# Getting started

Three sessions. The first takes about fifteen minutes and ends with a cold
email you would send. Stop anywhere: nothing resets, nothing reminds you, and
this page is where you pick it up again.

Each step is one task and one screen. Where a step raises a question, the
link under it goes to the one page that answers it.

The same ground is taught in the studio twice over. On **Home**, once your
first leads are in, a setup card lists five steps, each ticked by the thing it
asks for and each one press away, with *Take the one-minute tour* as its last
line. The card goes once all five are done. A colleague who joins a workspace
somebody else owns sees *Set up your seat* instead: three steps of their own
(joined, glance one company, bring in who you know), each ticked by what they
did themselves. And **Prospektor Academy**, under Learn in
[Settings](/settings/workspace), holds four short courses, each named after
what you have at the end: *Your first meeting from a cold company*, *Get
walked in by someone you know*, *Win your competitor’s customers* and *Make
every pitch sharper than the last*. Each card says how many steps it has and
how many minutes it takes. **Continue** at the top opens the step you are on.
A step shows you how, with a button for the screen it is about and **Mark as
done**. A step the studio can see you did (a glance run, a pitch finished, an
edit saved, a network imported, a competitor read, an outcome recorded) is
ticked for you, on whatever device you did it. A step you mark done here is
not emailed to you. Under the courses, **Asks that work** holds sentences
for the bar at the top, each with a blank; **Try it** puts one in the bar
with the blank selected, so you type the company and press Enter. Nothing
runs until you press the button on the screen it opens. *Take the one-minute
tour* is the last row. Nothing counts you and nothing resets. This page
stays.

## Before you start: open a workspace

A new workspace begins at [`/signup/`](/signup/). Sign in with
Google or your work email, type your company's website, say in one sentence
what Prospektor should find for you, pick monthly or yearly, and pay on
Stripe. You come straight back to Home, already signed in. While the studio
reads your site and looks for companies, Home shows what it has done so far and
asks one question: who already buys from you. Answer it there or leave it.
About a minute later your first three leads appear on Home, in the spot the
empty cards held. Anyone at your company's domain can sign in after you.

## Session 1: one email you would send

About fifteen minutes. You leave with a pitch on a real company and an email
in your own words.

### 1. Check the brief

The studio read your website and wrote who you hunt and how you sound. Every
pitch is written from that, so a wrong line here is a wrong line everywhere.

**Task:** open [Your brief](/settings/brief). Read *Who you are* and *How you
sound*. Fix one thing that is wrong.

If the top of the page says your brief was researched before you typed your
goal, press **Rescan your site** at its foot. Nothing changes until you accept
what comes back.

How-to: [the brief](/help/workspace).

<!-- Video slot, 40 seconds: Your brief opens, the reader finds one wrong line under How you sound, presses Edit, fixes it, saves. -->

### 2. Say who you already sell to

Two things happen the moment you do. Nobody on that list is ever pitched. And
the list steers what the studio suggests, because who buys from you is the
best evidence of who will.

**Task:** press **Answer** beside *Say who already buys from you* on Home's setup card, which opens
that one question on [Ideal customer](/settings/hunt), and name two or three
customers, each with why they are a good one. **Upload a list** under the box takes the
whole customer list as a CSV: an export straight out of your CRM works, because
the header row says which column is the company and which the website, and
every other column is ignored. The list lands on
[Do not contact](/suppress), and the count under the box opens it, so a wrong
row comes off there.

How-to: [Ideal customer](/help/workspace).

<!-- Video slot, 30 seconds: the customers box on Ideal customer, three names typed with a reason each, Save. -->

### 3. Run one company and make the email yours

**Task:** open [Leads for you](/leads) and press **Glance** on the top card.
Fifteen seconds later you have the fit score and the one thing. Press
**Prospekt →**. The run takes a few minutes; leave it and come back. When it
lands, open the sequence, press the ✎ pencil, rewrite it until you would
send it, and press **Save**.

On a free workspace the glance is part of your one run: pressing Glance opens
a screen that offers **Prospekt** on that company straight away.

The save is the step. An edit you save teaches the studio how you write, and
the next run starts from it. An edit you copy out and never save teaches it
nothing.

If Leads for you is still empty, name a company you already wanted to write to on
[Research prospekts](/pitch/new) instead.

How-to: [reading a pitch, and editing it](/help/pitches).

<!-- Video slot, 60 seconds: Glance pressed on a card, the fifteen-second read, Prospekt pressed, the six stages, the sequence opened, two sentences rewritten, Save, the "teaches the studio your voice" line. -->

Send that email.

## Session 2: teach it what happened

Ten minutes, some time in the first week, once a reply has come in or not.

### 4. Record what happened

This is the one thing that makes the tenth pitch better than the first. What
you record is read into every later pitch, call sheet and evaluation.

**Task:** in [Library](/library), press the badge on the card. It reads *What
happened?* until you set it. Pick one: found the right contact, had a meeting,
closed the deal, went quiet, not a fit, lost.

Paste the reply into **Add a note…** and the studio says what to do next.

How-to: [outcomes](/help/outcomes).

<!-- Video slot, 30 seconds: the badge on a Library card, the picker, a reply pasted into the note, the next step read back. -->

### 5. Hunt a competitor's customers

Their client list is your prospect list.

**Task:** open [Counterprospekt](/competitors). The competitors you named are
cards; press **Find their clients** on one, or add a rival in the last card. The
report lists who they sell to, each with the page that says so, and each
client is one press to a glance and then a pitch of your own.

How-to: [Counterprospekt](/help/screens).

<!-- Video slot, 45 seconds: a chip pressed, the report, the client list, Prospekt on one client. -->

## Session 3: warm paths

Ten minutes, plus the wait for a file from LinkedIn. Do it the day you want an
introduction rather than a cold email.

### 6. Bring in who you know

A cold email is the last resort. If somebody on your team already knows
somebody at the company, the studio finds that path and drafts both messages:
the ask to your contact, and the email for them to send on.

**Task:** on LinkedIn, Settings & Privacy, then Data privacy, then *Get a copy
of your data*, tick Connections, request the archive. LinkedIn emails a
`Connections.csv` in about ten minutes. Upload it on
[Your network](/network) under **Import LinkedIn connections**. Then open
[Warm intro](/intro) and name the company from step 3.

Email addresses in the file are dropped at import and never stored.

How-to: [your network, and warm paths](/help/network).

<!-- Video slot, 45 seconds: the LinkedIn export clicks, the upload, Warm intro with the company named, the two drafts. -->

## What this leaves out

The sidebar has seven rows and this path uses five. Decision-makers, Meeting
prep, Inbound, Your agents, sharing a pitch, the CRM push and the
Claude connector each have a page in this help and none of them is needed in the first week.
[The first visit, in detail](/help/first-visit) is the long version of the
screens above, and [the screens](/help/screens) is the map of all of them.

# The screens, and where each one lives

Every screen has a real URL. When pointing someone somewhere, use these
exact paths. A link opens the screen it names even when the opening questions
are still unanswered; those wait for you on Your brief, never in front of
somebody you sent somewhere.

| Screen | Path | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Leads for you | `/leads` | Companies the studio proposes pitching next, in white cards, one per reason. To ask for something else, describe it in the bar at the top, or paste a page that lists companies (an investor's portfolio, an exhibitor list): the companies on it land here, scored, in a row named after the page. The cards sit in rows, and every row says why it is there: *Like SplitPay, the deal you closed* for a deal recorded under What happened, *Like Northwind, one of your customers* for a customer named on Who we hunt, *Named on* the page you pasted, the search you typed under its own words, and one row for the bet outside what you have pressed on. A card sits in a deal's or a customer's row only when it was argued from that company; what the row's search finds that is not like it lands in the row with no heading. The screen shows three cards at a time. Glance at one, start it or cross it out, and the next takes its place; the studio searches again only when nothing is waiting behind them. A workspace that has recorded nothing sees one row with no heading, which is the shelf as it always was. The cross on a card teaches the row it sits in: the next search for that row is told what you turned down, and three crosses on a deal's or a customer's row rest it for a month, with *Keep looking* to wake it. Home shows the strongest card of each row. Under the cards, four presses complete the sentence *Or companies that*: *are hiring*, *just appointed a new leader*, *just raised money*, *just announced a partnership*. Each is the same search as typing those words into the bar, counts as one of the day's searches, and lands as a row headed by the words pressed; the presses are out of sight while the studio is already looking |
| Warm intro | `/intro` | *Who can introduce you?* The first of two tabs under the title *Warm intros*, **Introductions**: one box takes a company or a person, with **Find the path** beside it. Under the box, before you press anything, who you already know there, or that nobody is and the path would run through who they know. **Find the path** then maps your network against the company and answers with a count line (*2 paths, 1 strong*), the best path open and the rest folded, each with why, the tie verified against a page it read, and two drafts for the best path: the ask you send your contact (**Copy**, or **Open in Mail**, which opens your own mail app with the subject and the text filled in and no address) and the finished email for them to send on. Under the drafts, four chips say where the introduction stands: *Asked*, *They said yes*, *No*, *Meeting booked*; the last one opens Outcomes with the company filled in. Type the name of somebody in your network instead and the question turns round, *Who should they meet?*: who else in your network they should meet, what each side gets, and a double opt-in note. Under the card, **Introductions to pursue**: every company on your shelf or in your library that somebody in your network reaches, each row saying who can connect you and why (*Dana Ruiz can connect you · works there · will always introduce*), with **Pursue it** on each. Past asks sit under that. On a first visit the screen is one box and no tabs: paste who you know, one per line, press **Add them**, and the same card becomes the search |
| Lookalikes | `/lookalikes` | Name customers you already have; the studio finds more companies like them and puts them on Leads for you. A workspace can ask for 20 searches a day between this and the lead box |
| Decision-makers | `/people` | Two boxes: **Company** (a name or a domain) and **Who** (a role, a name, or a LinkedIn URL). *Company + role* finds who holds that desk (*CMO, Head of Partnerships*; leave Who blank for the desks that matter). *Person + a descriptor* looks one person up: a name at a company, a name with a role, or a pasted LinkedIn URL on its own, and the studio asks the contact vendors first and searches only to find where they work when you named no company. Each person comes with their LinkedIn, their work email where a vendor found one, and the phone press, in about a minute, and no pitch. A workspace can run 20 people searches a day. Company, Who and **Find people** sit on one line. What the searches found is shown by company: the newest company first, its people merged across searches in a table of *Name and role*, *Contact* and *Why them, now*, with a box to tick on each row. Under the table sit three links: *Write the pitch*, which opens Research prospekts with the company filled in; *Same roles at similar companies*, one press that finds up to three companies like it and looks for the same roles at each (five presses a day for a workspace; the companies land as companies of their own, each saying which one it is like); and *Download as CSV*, which downloads the rows you ticked. The other companies you looked up are a card of rows under it, *Other companies*: what you asked there and how many were named, and a click shows one. Under the finder, two rows appear once the workspace has the record behind them: *Find the CFO at other companies you pitched* (the role you ask for most, at the finished pitches in the Library nobody has asked it at; one press runs that people search) and *People you can get introduced to* (the best person in your imported network at a company on your shelf or in your Library, with the tie; one press opens Warm intros with the company filled in). A cross hides a company from a row |
| Open search | `/search` | Type who you want into the bar at the top, in your own words (*Property managers in the Midwest with more than 10k doors* is the example under **Try**), and press Enter. The words become filters, shown as chips you can remove one at a time; removing one searches again without it. A filter no database holds, such as a number of doors, is a chip with a globe that reads *not checked yet*. The people come from a contact database in seconds, 25 at a time, with **Load more** under the table. Two tabs: **People** (the person and their role, the company with its size and city, Email, Phone, and *Way in*, someone in your imported network who is at that company) and **Companies** (the company, a **Check** link that reads it for the filter no database holds, its fit if your Library already has it, and how many people the search found there). Tick rows, or the box in the header for all of them, and a dark bar opens at the foot. On People it offers **Find emails**, **Find phones** and **Write to them** (the pitch for those people's companies); on Companies, **Find decision-makers** and **Write the pitch**. Emails and phones fill into their cells as they are found, through the same lookups Decision-makers uses: a phone is counted against your month only when one is found, and a workspace can look up 100 emails and 50 phones a day. Nobody on your do-not-contact list, or at a company on it, is looked up. A workspace can run 10 searches a day; each removed chip and each **Load more** is one. The page lives in the tab: a reload goes back to Home |
| Your agents | `/agents` | Describe what you want done, in one sentence, and the studio builds the agent that does it. It picks the door (find leads, lookalikes, a glance, a pitch, decision-makers, a competitor report, or a standing watch on one rival) and fills in what that door needs from your brief. A watch reports what that company publicly did since the last look, each move dated, sourced, and with one line on what to do about it. The agent is kept, so next time it is one press, and a sentence that says how often ("every Monday") makes it standing, running itself until you press Stop. When a sentence names something the studio cannot do yet, it says so instead of doing the nearest thing. Reached from **Ideal customer** |
| Research prospekts | `/pitch/new` | Three tabs. **One company** is the form: company name or domain, then Glance; a contact, notes, motion and value angle sit behind More options, and *Researched lately* lists the newest three. **Lookalikes** finds companies like your customers. **A whole list** pitches up to a hundred at once |
| Running | `/running` | Runs in flight, as a strip at the head of Library while something runs, and where a run you start opens; Watch drops into the live terminal; a stuck run can be dismissed, a live one stopped. The address lands on Library |
| Home | `/start` | Where signing in lands you. Your name, and one box whose placeholder shows what to type. Say what you want to do and it opens the screen that does it, with the name you gave already in its box. Paste a company's website address and it opens Research with that company. Nothing runs until you press the button there. Ask about your own record (*which pitches went quiet*, *what did Acme object to*) and the answer appears under the bar in a few lines, read from the outcomes you recorded and the pitches you finished; under it, one row per company it drew on, which opens that pitch or the record. When the record does not hold the answer it says so and names nothing; nothing runs and nothing is written. Any other question opens the support chat. Under the box, five chips for the asks people type most: *Give me leads*, *Property managers in the Midwest with more than 10k doors* (an example of the open search, `/search`), *Who buys from a competitor*, *Who can introduce me*, *Answer an inbound lead*. Then what is waiting as pills you can press (runs going, runs stopped, outcomes to record), three at most and none when nothing is. Under those, the three leads worth a look: the top three of Leads for you, each a score, a name, a site and the one thing, with **Glance** and the ×. While the studio is still looking, three empty cards and one line; before it has looked, one button, **Get leads**. The screen asks you nothing: what the studio still wants to know is on Your brief. The title reads *Welcome* and your first name while the setup cards show, and *Home* after that. Once a week, where the deployment has it turned on, **your weekly report** opens over Home on the first visit of the week (from your second week; a line under the chips opens it any time): what works, what is missing, the two things standing between you and the next meeting with one press each and *Not relevant*, four numbers (outcomes recorded, leads waiting, pitches finished, spent this week), and a box that asks the support chat about the week. Nothing in it is written by a model; every line is read off your workspace |
| Library | `/library` | The searches your companies came from, one row each, named by the studio from what you asked and renamed with the pencil; press a row to open its cards, strongest fit first, with unread markers. Press a card to open it, its badge to record what happened, and its ⋯ menu for Meeting prep or to move it to another search. A single search is no list: its cards are the screen |
| A search | `/library/<id>` | One search open in the Library, as a panel to the right of the list of searches: its name, the pencil that renames it, and its companies, strongest fit first. Press another row to switch; × closes the panel. On a narrow screen the panel sits under the list |
| A pitch | `/pitches/<id>` | One run: live while it works, the finished pitch after |
| Outcomes | `/outcomes` | The full history for every prospect: notes, the timeline, and "Make sense of this", which reads a record back. A tab of Settings, because what you record here is what every later pitch is written from. Recording an outcome does not need this screen: that is a press on the lead itself |
| Counterprospekt | `/competitors` | Your competitors' clients are your next leads. **Your competitors** is a card per competitor: the ones you have read say how many clients were found, with *See their clients*; the ones we think compete for your customers, and the ones named on your brief, say *Not read yet*, with **Find their clients**. A competitor saved twice (botika.com and botika.io) is one card. The last card is **Add a competitor**: type a name or a website and press **Find their clients**. Under it, **Leads from your competitors** is one table of every read competitor's clients: the company and where it was found, whose client it is, its fit, and one press. Best fit first: a company has a fit once you have glanced it. The press is **Glance**, then **Write the pitch** once glanced, **Watch** while a pitch is being written and **Open the pitch** once it lands. *All* shows the whole table |
| A competitor report | `/competitors/<id>` | One competitor: live while it researches, the finished report after. *‹ Your competitors* goes back. The head names them, their site and how long ago it was read, with *Not a competitor* and *Read again*. Three tiles take your side: their strength, their weakness, how you win. Then **Their clients**, each with the page that names them as a source, its fit and one press, the same press as on the table. The head of the list says how many were read of about how many their site names, and *Read more* under it reads the rest for the price of another run; a run reads up to forty. The four cards behind the tiles (they sell · their positioning · their customers · our read) and the sources fold at the foot |
| Inbound | `/evaluate` | Two tabs, Reply and Prepare a call. Reply: paste what a lead sent, get the reply to send in your voice, with whether they are worth your time and what to ask before quoting behind it |
| Prepare a call | `/prep` | The second tab of Inbound: one sheet for a specific upcoming call, goal, framing, talking points, the likely objection with an answer |
| Your network | `/network` | The second tab of Warm intros: the people who make the introductions. Four totals under the tabs (*People*, *Companies*, *Strong ties*, *Last import*), then **Who introduces you**: the people from your pasted lists, the people at customers you won (read out of your CRM with the won deals), and your strongest LinkedIn ties, each with two chips, **Always introduces** and **Might introduce**; one press marks, a second clears, and every ranking in the studio reads the mark. Then **Imports**, one row per import with how many people and when; **Add people ›** on that card opens the paste box and the LinkedIn, address-book and post doors, which are open on their own while nothing is imported |
| Do not contact | `/suppress` | A page of Settings: the standing rules that rule companies out, and the named list of companies and people this workspace will never approach. The newest twenty-five are shown with the count beside them, because the list can be uploaded whole. A customer named on Ideal customer joins it on its own |
| Ideal customer | `/settings/hunt` | Seven answers: who your dream customer would be, what you look for, where and how big, your customers, what you want more of, and your competitors. Asked one per screen while most are unanswered, then shown as a list with each row marked Missing, Check, Add more or done. *Upload a list* under the customers question takes the whole customer list as a CSV, read in your browser, and a connected Lightfield can be imported from instead on Workspace settings. A customer named here joins Do not contact and is never approached, and the competitors are the chips on Counterprospekt |
| Your brief | `/settings/brief` | The brief every deliverable is written from, in short: who you are, how you sound, what has worked, and what never goes out, three lines each. The whole document is one press away, and the questions the studio still has are folded at the foot |
| Profile and Notifications | `/settings/account` | Yours rather than the workspace's, the first two rows of the You card on Settings. **Profile**: passkeys, the recovery phone, the language the studio writes in, Log out, and the Danger zone last. **Notifications**: which emails the studio sends you and how else it may reach you |
| Settings | `/settings` | The hidden half of the product: one page of four cards, each a list of rows, and every row opens its own page. **This workspace**: Name and website (the name, the website, whose studio this is, at `/settings/workspace`), Plan (pause or cancel). **What Prospektor knows**: Your brief, Ideal customer, Outcomes, Do not contact, Brand (colours, the standing deck, then the deliverable stylesheet). **People and apps**: Team (who can sign in, one row per person, and your own role), Sub-accounts (agencies only: every client workspace, one press to switch), Sharing (every link the team has sent, and Revoke), Connectors (the apps connected to this workspace, tokens and Slack; the owner's alone). **You**: Profile, Notifications, Academy (four short courses on your own leads, asks to try in the bar, and the tour), Affiliate (refer a workspace and earn 20% of what it pays for twelve months; *Coming soon* until the programme is on). Each page opens under its own title with one *Settings* link back, and holds its settings in white cards, each a title and its rows, with no line explaining the card. The old `/shares` address opens the workspace page |
| Upgrade | `/upgrade` | Free workspaces only: what your one full pitch bought, and the way to the rest of your list. Your brief, pitch and leads stay readable behind it |
| Who opens which door | `/paths` | Agencies only: one console across every client workspace you hold. It reads **your** network against every company those workspaces are working on (their suggestions as well as their finished pitches) and ranks the doors, best first. Somebody who works at the company beats somebody whose note mentions it, whatever else you know about them. Free to open and no research runs: pressing a row switches you into that client's workspace and opens the introduction ask there, so the drafts come out in their voice. Reached from **Your network** |
| Portfolio uploads | `/portfolio` | Agencies only: how your last portfolio upload is going, and the ones before it |

The sidebar carries eight rows under four questions, and every row is
something you do to a company. **Home** first. Under *Who?*: **Leads for you**
(with how many are waiting), **Research** and **Counterprospekt**. Under *Who at
them?*: **Decision-makers**. Under *Who can walk you in?*: **Warm intros**. Under
*What to say?*: **Library** and **Inbound**. Above them, one coral button,
**Prospekt a company**, which opens Research prospekts. At the foot, **Help**
(the support chat) and **Settings**, then your name.

Three rows hold more than one screen, as tabs at the top: **Research** is
Research prospekts and Lookalikes; **Warm intros** is
Introductions and Your network; **Inbound** is the reply and Prepare a call.
Everything that teaches the studio rather than uses it is under **Settings**,
which opens as one page of four cards: This workspace (Name and website, Plan),
What Prospektor knows (Your brief, Ideal customer, Outcomes, Do not contact,
Brand), People and apps (Team, Sub-accounts, Sharing, Connectors) and You
(Profile, Notifications, Academy, Affiliate). Each row opens its own page, with
one Settings link back at the top. Every screen keeps its own address, so a
link to `/people` or `/settings/hunt` still opens that screen with its row lit.

On a new workspace, **Home** carries the getting-started path. While the
studio sets itself up, a card says what it has done so far (read your website,
drafted your brief, searching for companies that fit, scoring the best of
them), and a second card asks who already buys from you. Once the first three
leads land, both go and a setup card takes their place: five steps in the order
a customer takes them (read your website, say what to find, glance one company,
say who already buys from you, bring in who you know), each ticked by the thing
it asks for rather than by a press, each open one with its one action, and
*Take the one-minute tour* as the last line. It is gone once every step is done.
The tour never opens on its own.

A colleague who joins a workspace somebody else owns sees *Set up your seat*
instead, with three steps of their own: joined, glance one company, and bring
in who you know. Each is ticked by what that person did, not by the owner's
work. In one of the few old workspaces with nobody recorded as its owner,
everybody sees the five steps, with a line under them asking you to write to us
so we set one.

**Your account** is **Profile**, the first row of the You card on Settings, and the
same page opens from the workspace menu at the sidebar's head; those settings
are yours and follow you into every workspace you belong to.

## On a phone

The sidebar is a sheet. Press the button at the top left and it slides in
carrying the same rows, the workspace switcher at its head and Help, Settings
and your name at its foot. Pressing a row opens that screen and closes the sheet
behind it; so does the dimmed area beside it, and so does Escape on a keyboard.

**Research prospekts** is the round button at the bottom right instead of a row
in the sheet. It is the one thing most people open the studio on a phone to do, so it
is one press from wherever you are, and it steps aside once you are on it.

Four screens are reached from inside another rather than from the sidebar,
because that is where you are when you want them. **Your agents** is a link on
Ideal customer. **Running** is a
strip at the head of Library while something runs. **Do not contact**, the
standing rules and the named list of who not to approach, is its own page
under Settings. **Sharing** is a card on Settings.

**Who opens which door** reads only the workspaces you can already open. It is
your own memberships intersected with the workspaces you created, so a client
who has since removed you, or one you detached, is not on it. It maps your
network **down** to their companies and never reads their network back up.

**Warm intro** used to be a panel you could only reach on a finished
pitch. It still appears there (a pitch you have already run shows its paths
without being asked) but the screen above is the way in when you have not run
one, and it is the only place the second direction lives.

**Decision-makers** is the people search on its own, with no pitch attached.
It is the search a finished pitch runs for its decision-maker list and the
same email lookup, so the list is the one you would have had at the end of a
Prospekt without buying the rest. *Write the pitch* under a finished list is
the way to the rest, with the company already filled in.

Two old addresses still work: `/` opens Home, and `/shares` opens the
workspace page of Settings. `/settings` is the Settings page itself.

**Counterprospekt** deserves one more sentence, because its rule is strict:
a report names a company as the competitor's client **only when a page the
run actually read says so**, and every entry links that page. A claimed
client without a source is left out and counted, never shown. The competitors
you named at onboarding are cards that have not been read yet; one press runs
that report, and the last card is for anyone else. Finished
reports also appear in the Library, and a company on your suppress list can
still be analyzed (the list says who not to *approach*) so a suppressed
company in their client list simply gets no pitch button.

### What a report says

A finished report opens on **three tiles that take your side** (*their
strength*, *their weakness*, and *how you win*), then their clients as your
prospect list. The four cards behind the three tiles (they sell · their
positioning · their customers · our read, at most three one-line bullets each)
open on one press at the foot; the three tiles are their summary.

*How you win* is the one line no competitor's website could ever answer: it is
written from **your brief**, pointed at the weakness above it. If your brief
does not yet say enough for the studio to name a real edge, that line comes
back as a bracketed gap rather than a slogan; brackets are always work still
owed, never an answer. Filling in more of your brief is what turns it into a
sentence you can use.

Reports run before this existed have no three tiles and are not re-run for
them; press *Read again* if you want them.

The workspace switcher sits at the sidebar's head: click your workspace
name to switch workspaces, set **Appearance** (light / dark / system),
create a client workspace or upload a whole
portfolio of them (agencies), or sign out. An agency workspace is tagged
**(Agency)** in that list with its client workspaces indented under it.
Support is the round button at the bottom right, on every screen.
On a narrow window the sidebar collapses to its icons.

# Pitches: runs, results, editing

## The glance: is this company worth my time?

**Glance** takes about fifteen seconds and answers one question: is this
company worth a full run?

It is on every list of companies the studio shows you ([Leads](/), the
lookalikes on a finished pitch, a Counterprospekt report's client list) and on
[Research prospekts](/pitch/new). On Leads it is the card's one press, because a shelf
is for triage; **Prospekt**, the full run, is the purchase you make from the
glance. A glance goes in your Library like any other reading, and the
shelf stops offering that company; Suggested never proposes work you have
already done, so what is on it is always what you have not looked at yet.

What comes back is one card: a fit score out of 100, the single argument the
case rests on, two or three signals for and against, and the **roles** worth
approaching. It searches for the company and opens
their own site to do it, capped at three searches and two pages, and the card
says how long it took against the fifteen-second ceiling so you can hold us to
it.

**It comes back whole, or it says so.** A reading that arrives missing part of
its answer is asked for a second time and then stopped, rather than shown to
you as a score with nothing under it. The one exception is the second score,
the buyer reading: a glance that has its score, its argument and its signals
but no second reading is kept, with that reading marked *not scored* rather
than invented.

**It knows what you sell.** The glance reads your brief's facts and your fit
thesis before it scores, so a target is judged as a company that might buy
from you, never as a company that resembles you. A note you type on the run
outranks the brief: if you know a company is a customer in the making, say so,
and the score follows. The card says in one line what it made of your note,
and a score that goes against it is asked for a second time: either the number
moves, or that line says what the studio read that outweighed you.

**Your brief sets who comes first.** The size, stage and kinds of buyer you
gave are weighed, and none of them rules a company out by itself. A company
bigger or further along than your brief names loses some points and keeps its
case: where it would still buy, the card calls it a possible upmarket fit and
says how to pitch it. Only the rules you set about who never to approach take
a company off the table.

**It is kept.** Every finished glance gets a card in the
[Library](/library) (the score and the desks it named) marked
**Glance** so it is never mistaken for a pitch. Press the card and you are
back on the glance, with the same presses on it: name the people, write a
piece, or Prospekt. The card also carries **Prospekt →** on its own, because
that is the one thing a glance is missing. A finished pitch
carries no button, since pressing it is what opens it. It has its own link,
and it tags and filters like anything else there. Once the full pitch is
finished it takes the glance's place in the list rather than sitting beside
it: one company, one card. Nothing is deleted: the glance keeps its own link
and is still there while the run is out, and if the run fails. Run a company
a second time and the newer run takes the card the same way; the older run
keeps its link.

**How many a day.** A workspace can run 100 glances a day, and each member
50 of them. Writing one piece off a glance or a pitch (a one-pager, a deck)
counts against 20 a day for the workspace.

**Two pages buys the front of a business, not all of it.** Where a company
plainly runs more than one line, the card says which one it scored: *"Scored
as a consumer app; it may also have a B2B channel this glance did not read."*
That line is the reason to buy the full run rather than to trust a low score.

**It names roles, never people.** Naming a person needs a source, finding a
source needs searches, and searches are what a fifteen-second answer does not
have. Naming them is the next press.

## Outside your brief, and still a buyer

**Every company gets two readings, and they answer different questions.** The
score at the top of a pitch is *how well does this match the brief you wrote*.
Beside it the studio asks a second question it does not show unless the answer
surprises: *would this company buy what you sell, whoever your brief names*.

Most of the time the two agree, and you see nothing extra. They come apart in
one direction: a company your brief does not describe, which would buy the work
anyway. Then the number at the top of the pitch is the buyer score, labelled *a
buyer, outside what you hunt for*, and the summary carries both numbers with one
sentence on what they would be buying. The same head leads the glance. A brief
score of 28 is a correct answer to a question you did not ask, and it used to be
the biggest thing on the screen.

This exists because a narrow brief was throwing away good prospects and calling
them bad ones. A brief that says *law firms in Toronto* scores a bank at 8, and
8 is the correct answer to the question it was asked. It is the wrong answer to
the question you actually have, especially when that bank is on a competitor's
own client list, which is the strongest evidence there is that a company buys
this work: they already bought it, from your rival.

**One press widens the brief, and only a press does.** Where the readings
disagree, the studio names the *kind* of company it found, such as *banks and
financial firms in the same city*, and offers **Always look for these**. That
writes one line to what you hunt for, every later search reads it, and it comes
off again on [Ideal customer](/settings/hunt). Nothing is added without the press.

**Three things it deliberately does not do.** It does not change your leads:
the shelf stays governed by your brief until you have widened it yourself. It
is not a softer score, so a company that would not buy scores low on both. And
it never reaches past a **no**: anyone on your suppress list stays suppressed,
and a rule you wrote about who you will never approach still decides first.

## Ask for the leads you want

**Describe them in the bar at the top.** *"mid-market property managers in the
Southeast running class A and B units"*, *"agencies that already resell Shopify
apps"*, *"anyone hiring a Head of Partnerships this quarter"*. The bar opens
[Your agents](/agents) with your sentence already in its box; press **Build it**
and the search it runs puts the companies on Leads for you, with the same Glance
press every other lead has. Nothing runs until you press.

**Or paste a page that lists them.** An investor's portfolio, a conference's
exhibitor list, a partner directory: describe what you want from it with the
address in the sentence. The studio opens that page, takes the companies it
names, scores the strongest of them against your brief and puts up to eight on
the shelf, in a row headed by the page they came from. Nothing the page does not
name is added, and a page the studio cannot open adds nothing. A page read
counts as one of the day's lead searches.

It is the fastest way to two different things:

**The studio has your market slightly wrong.** Rather than correcting it one
company at a time, say what you actually want and get it.

**You want to try something new.** A market you have never worked in, a
one-off idea, a client who asked for something odd. Type it, look at what comes
back, and nothing about your workspace changes.

**Asking never changes your brief.** That is deliberate: most of what people
type here is an experiment, and an experiment that quietly rewrote what the
studio hunts would make the box risky to use for the thing it is best at.

**Ask who moved, not only who fits.** *"Companies that just raised a Series
A"*, *"anyone who opened a UK office this summer"*, *"agencies that changed
their head of growth recently"*, a request that names a time is answered with
companies that moved in one. A card that found something says so on one line,
*"Raised a $40m Series B · 14 Aug"*, and that line opens the page it was read
on. Most companies have not moved and their cards say nothing about when; a
fit score is about whether a company is right, and this is about whether today
is the day.

**We never guess a date.** A move is on the card only when the search read the
event and the day it happened on a page, with the page linked. Nothing older
than six months counts as news.

**Prospekt a company that moved and the move writes the email.** The run is
handed what happened and the day it happened, and inside two months that is the
opening line: why this note is arriving today, in the reader's terms. Older
than that it argues the case and never opens on it: a note congratulating
somebody on something months behind them reads worse than one that never
mentions it. The run checks the move still holds while it reads their pages, and
drops it if what it finds says otherwise.

**A company you typed in gets the same treatment.** The full run looks for a
dated move itself while it reads their pages, so a company you found somewhere
else (Research prospekts, a portfolio list, a finished pitch's lookalikes) can still
open on why today. Same bar: read on a page, dated, linked, inside six months;
where the run already has a move, the fresher of the two wins.

## Build an agent from a description

**`/agents`: say what you want done, and the studio builds the thing that does
it.** One sentence: *"find agencies in Berlin that already run paid search"*,
*"read Signaliz and tell me who they sell to"*, *"who should I be calling at
Northline?"* The studio picks the door (find leads, lookalikes, a glance, a
pitch, decision-makers, a competitor report) and fills in what that door needs
from your brief.

**The agent is kept.** Next time it is one press, and the list shows when each
one last ran.

**Watch a competitor, and it tells you what to do about each move.** *"Watch
Signaliz every week"* builds a standing watch: the card lists what that company
publicly did since the last look (a launch, a price change, a funding round, a
partnership), each with its date, a link, and one line on what to do about it.
Nothing public since the last watch is a real answer and the card says so. It
reports what a *company* did, never what a person did.

**Say how often and it runs itself.** *"Check Signaliz every Monday"* is a
standing agent: the card shows when it next runs, and **Stop** ends it. Three
agents per workspace may stand at once, and a schedule needs a subscription;
a free workspace keeps the words and the card says so. To add a schedule to an
agent that has none, describe it again with the cadence in the sentence.

**It never invents what you did not say.** *"Watch our biggest rival"* names no
rival, so the card asks which company and nothing else.

**And it says when it cannot.** A sentence the studio has no verb for is
answered as one, not routed to the nearest thing. The agent is kept anyway, so
what you asked for is on the record.

There is nothing else to configure. No model to choose, no tools to switch on,
no prompt to edit: the brief you already wrote is the configuration, which is
why one sentence is enough.

**A standing request lives on your brief.** Anything kept there is listed on
[Ideal customer](/settings/hunt) under *What we keep looking for*, every search
reads it, and a cross removes it.

**What it will not do:** get past your suppress list, your disqualifiers, or
companies you have already been shown. Asking for something new widens where
the studio looks; it never overrides who you have said no to.

## Is the score wrong? Tell the studio why

**Press the score.** If a company is a better fit than the number says, the
score itself opens one question: *what did we get wrong?* Type a sentence and
press **Re-score**.

Two things happen, and the second one is the point.

**This company is scored again**, in about fifteen seconds, with what you said
taken as given. The new number is earned rather than typed: you do not set the
score, you correct the thing the score was wrong about.

**And the studio learns the part that was about you.** Most corrections contain
two things at once: *"Bozzuto is an excellent fit; we serve class A and B units
**and** luxury operators, we are not limited to lower-income housing."* The
first half is about that one company and stays on its record, where the full
pitch and the call sheet read it as your call. If a pitch still scores against
it, the pitch's checks say so. The second half is about **you**, and it goes on
your brief, where every future glance, every company the studio suggests, and
every pitch it writes will read it.

That is why a wrong score is worth thirty seconds. Fixing the number helps one
lead; correcting the premise changes what the studio goes looking for.

A green line tells you exactly what was learned, and **Undo** takes it straight
back off if it is not what you meant. Your corrections are listed on **Your
brief**, where you can edit or delete any of them.

**Or say they are a competitor.** If the company competes with you, say so in
the same box. They are not scored again, because how good a prospect they are
is the wrong question about a company you sell against. They go on your rival
list instead, so the studio stops offering them and hunts the market around
them. **Undo** takes that back, and they are listed on **Do not contact**.

**What makes a good correction:** a fact about your company that would still be
useful for a company nobody has mentioned yet. *"We sell to CFOs, not office
managers"* teaches the studio something. *"This one is good"* only fixes this
one.

## Name the people: one press on the glance

**Name the people** sits under the roles on the glance card. One press buys
the searches the glance would not spend: about a minute, capped at four pages
and four searches, and the roles become named people, each with the source
that supports the name, and a LinkedIn link only where a profile was actually
read. A role nobody could be sourced for is then asked of the contact
vendors, who answer with the person who holds it and their profile; where
they have nobody either, the role stays a role, with a null name, because a
guessed name is worse than none. A named person without a profile link is
looked up the same way, so the badge beside the name is their profile
wherever a vendor knows it. People on your workspace's
suppress list are never returned, and a company on it refuses the press the
way it refuses a run. The card prints the timing against the sixty-second
ceiling, the way the glance prints its fifteen.

## What to send: one piece at a time, or everything

Under the glance you decide what to buy. **What to send** offers each piece
(pitch deck, one-pager, sequence, proposal) as its own press: one call,
under 90 seconds, written in your voice with everything your workspace has
taught the studio, and written to read as a person wrote it: no dashes, no
stock phrases, plain verbs. Pressing one opens the pitch straight away (the glance's
score and argument are already on it) and the piece lands under *The pitch*
while you watch. Each further piece is another press in the format menu; the pitch
grows as you buy, is saved to your library like any other, and every piece
is editable and shareable the moment it lands. A piece a pitch does not have
yet always shows its press, on staged pitches and on full runs where you
unticked it alike. The compliance check runs on the whole pitch after every
press.

A glance itself is not saved to your library and does not use up anything.
Press **Prospekt →** on the card and the six-step run starts on the same
company: deeper research, everything written at once.

## Starting a full run

[Research prospekts](/pitch/new) takes a company name, a bare domain, or both. Behind
**More options**, all optional: notes, a point of contact, which outputs to
write, the motion to argue for and the value angle to lead with (the last two
come from your workspace's own brief). Notes are read as your word on the
company: where they say something the brief does not, they win, and the score
follows them. Until you have edited **Your brief** yourself, the studio treats
what it drafted there as its own reading rather than your rule, so a line it
wrote about who is too large or too small can lower a score but never
disqualify a company on its own. The motion
on a finished pitch is one your brief lists, in your own words. A brief
that lists none is scored as a direct case (every company judged as a buyer
of what you sell) and the studio never argues a reseller, affiliate or
partner route the brief does not name; where that is the only case, it says
so and the score stays low. The same happens when your brief lists motions
your goal does not support: a goal that hunts companies to sell to, over a
list of partnership routes, is argued as the goal and the pitch comes back
with no motion set. If you see that, the list is stale. Edit it on **Your
brief**, or rescan.

Once you have named a company, the **Prospekt** button says how long one
takes: `Prospekt · ~7 min`. The number is the middle of your own
workspace's finished runs, so it reflects your brief, your deliverables and
how much reading your targets need. It appears once three
runs have finished; before that we do not know yet, and would rather say
nothing than guess. Runs are included in your plan; the minutes are the only
thing a run costs you.

Before anything else, the studio works out **who the company actually is**
from its own website: it opens the site, reads what they sell and to whom,
and rules out same-named businesses. The pitch is then researched, scored
and drafted against that settled identity.

## While it runs

**A run starts on your Library, not on a screen of its own.** Press Prospekt
or Glance and the Library opens with the run's line at the head of its
Running card: the company, the step it is on and what it last did. You can
go anywhere else in the studio while it works. A glance opens itself when it
lands, as long as you are still on the Library; a pitch, or a glance you left,
says it is ready with an **Open it** press. **Watch** on the line, or the
run's own `/pitches/<id>` link, opens the full live view described below.

A run takes a few minutes (the button that started it said how many, measured
off your own finished runs) and shows six named stages: understand, research,
score, draft, people, check, with what each stage is actually doing ("2
searches · 9 sources read"; the counts are that step's own work). The stages
are not strictly single-file: the decision-maker search needs only the
confirmed target, so it runs alongside the drafting rather than after it;
**both steps light up at once** while that happens, the foot names both
("Steps 2 & 5 of 6 · BDR + SDR agents"), and step 5 ticks done the moment its
list is ready, even while the drafts are still being written. The drafts
themselves are written **side by side**: each deliverable is its own call,
the same call its press on a finished pitch makes, so the drafting step
takes as long as its slowest piece, not the sum of all of them. A piece that
fails does not fail the run; the finished pitch ships without it, and its
row in the format menu holds the press to write it. There is no
percentage bar on purpose: research is one
stage of six, and a long read would sit at 17% looking dead. The clock counts
from when the run started, not from when you opened the screen, so coming back
to a run four minutes in says four minutes. When the draft lands, the terminal
ends with **where the time went**: each step's own clock, from the run's own
record, including what ran in parallel.

**A company the studio already researched is not researched again.** Research
on a target is kept for a month and shared across every workspace on the
deploy, so a rerun (or another workspace pitching the same company) starts
from the settled identity, and the more Prospektor is used the more of your
research is already done. The run says so ("Already researched today: …,
read once for every workspace on Prospektor"), and it caps its remaining
reading to a small, named freshness budget ("Research already settled: capped
at 3 pages · 2 searches"): recent news and anything time-sensitive, never a
re-read of pages it already holds. What crosses is the reading of a public
website and nothing else; the box carries nothing about the workspace that
paid for it, and nothing of your brief, your client or your edits ever reaches
it.

**The steps on the left keep what they found.** The terminal on the right
streams the run as it happens and scrolls; the steps beside it fold each
finished step into a summary that stays for the rest of the run: what your
brief brought to it, who the company turned out to be and which same-named
businesses were ruled out, every page it opened (each one a link you can open
and check) and every search it ran, then each deliverable as it is written. By
the last step that column is the run's own account of itself, and you can read
it without having watched.

Under the six, greyed out, are the three things that come after a finished
pitch: send or share it, prep the call it books, record what happened. They
are signposts to screens you already have, not steps this run takes.

**Each step says who is doing it.** The right-hand column of the rail names the
agent working on that step, and the foot of the run names the one working now.
It is a GTM team, and these are the five:

- **BDR agent** brings you companies worth pitching. Opens each target's own
  website before anything else and works out who they actually are, not who
  shares their name; scores fit against your brief; suggests the next ones
  worth your time and names the ones it ruled out. *(research, score)*
- **SDR agent** finds you the way in. Names the decision-makers with a source
  behind every name and a confidence rating on each, and leaves a blank rather
  than inventing one; then finds the warm path through your network. *(people)*
  Companies share names, so a name is checked against the company the BDR
  agent settled on before it reaches you: someone a source places at a
  same-named company elsewhere is left off, and *confirmed* is only given
  where the source ties the person to this company's own site; the rest read
  *likely*. Fewer names, every one of them at the right company. And when the
  search comes back empty but the research already read profile pages naming
  people here, those people are on the list, with a short second look to
  confirm their roles.
- **AE agent** writes what you send. Drafts the deck, the one-pager, the
  proposal and the sequence in your voice, grounded in what has already
  worked for you; preps the call it books. When somebody at the company
  reacted to or commented on one of your posts (pasted under
  [Your network](/network)), the opener says what they reacted to.
  *(draft, and prep afterwards)*
- **Sales Ops agent** checks the work before you see it. Reads the finished
  draft back against the rules and flags anything that broke one: an invented
  number, a fabricated person, a banned word, a company the research already
  ruled out. It never rewrites your copy; it makes the problem visible next to
  the thing that has it. *(check)*
- **RevOps agent** remembers what worked. Every outcome you record and every
  edit you save goes into the next run, so run 100 is not run 1. *(learn)*

Two steps carry no agent, and both are deliberate. **Understand the request**
is your own brief read back; you wrote it, so nothing else takes credit for
it. And **send or share it** says *You*: the agents research and draft, and you
send. Nothing here has your relationships, and nothing signs your name.

**The rail's order is the run's order.** A run drafts the deliverables before
it names the decision-makers, so the AE agent appears above the SDR agent on
the rail even though a sales team would introduce them the other way round.
That is the true order the work happens in, and the rail shows it rather than a
tidier one.

Setting up a workspace shows a shorter, three-step rail with no agents on it.
That job is the studio reading *your* site to draft *your* brief, not a pitch,
and it should never look like one.

**You can leave.** The worker runs in the background; [Running](/running)
lists every run in flight with Watch to drop back in. A run nothing has been
heard from in twenty minutes is marked stopped and offers **Dismiss**; a run
still working offers **Stop** (confirmed, because it kills real work). There is no
pause.

**Busy moments are retried, and a failure is a fresh start.** The model
provider occasionally has a busy moment; the run says so in its log, backs
off and retries by itself; nothing you entered is lost. A run that fails
anyway says why in one plain sentence and offers two buttons, there and in
*Did not finish*: **Rerun** starts a fresh attempt at the same target with
the same ticked deliverables (a glance that failed reruns as a glance, never
as the full run), and **Share this bug with Prospektor** sends
that run's error and step log to the Prospektor team for analysis, only
when you press it, never on its own.

**Everybody reads every run; your own are yours to manage.** Stopping,
archiving or deleting a run somebody else started, or calling off their
batch, needs the owner or admin role in the workspace. Reading it never
does. (The roles are in [Workspace settings](/help/workspace).)

## A whole list at once

The **A whole list** tab on Research (Beast Mode, until it had a tab of its
own): upload a CSV or paste one company per line
(`Company name, website`, the website optional; with a header row the columns
are read by name, so a CRM export works as it is) and **Run the list** queues
every row through the same pipeline. Up to 100 companies per batch, three
running at once, each landing in the Library like any other pitch. The CSV
is parsed in your browser and never uploaded. A free workspace runs its one
full pitch from the form above, one company at a time; a batch is the rest of
your list, and pressing it opens [Upgrade](/help/first-visit).

**One email at the end, not one per run.** Close the tab; when the last
target lands, the studio emails whoever started the batch: which companies
scored 75% or higher, named, with their own scores and the angle each run
chose, a link straight to each of them, and how many runs landed out of how
many you queued. If nothing cleared 75% the mail says so and names the
closest instead, because that is also the answer. Fifty targets are never
fifty emails, and it is off in one click from the mail itself or in
[Workspace settings](/help/workspace).

## Searches: the Library's rows

Every company in the Library got there through a search: a lookalike search,
an ask typed into the lead box, a page you pasted, a list you uploaded, a
rival's client list from a Counterprospekt report. The Library lists those
searches as a table, one row each: how many companies it holds, the best fit
among them and when it last moved. Press a row to open it; inside, each
company is a row with its fit, where it stands and who started it, strongest
fit first.

**The studio names each search from what you asked.** *Like SplitPay* for a
lookalike search, your ask as you typed it, the page's own name, the name you
gave an uploaded list or its day (*Batch, 29 Sep*), *Rival Inc's clients* for
a report. Two rows are standing: **Found for you** holds what the shelf found
on its own, and **One at a time** holds companies typed on Research or sent by
a machine token.

**Rename a search with one press.** The pencil beside the name turns it into
a box; Enter or **Save** keeps it, Escape puts the old name back. Names are
free text, shared with everyone in the workspace, editable by any of them,
never sent anywhere, and kept with the workspace.

**Move a company with ⋯ → Move to…** on its card, for the one time a company
belongs in a different search than the one that found it. **New search…** at
the foot of that list makes one and files the company under it.

A dot before a row's name means something in it is unread. One search is no
list: while the Library holds a single search, its cards are the screen. The
Running strip above the rows says an uploaded list's own name while it runs.

**Glances land the same way.** A glance lands in the Library beside your
pitches, marked **Glance**, under the search that found the company.

## Reading the result

A pitch opens on one card and three tabs. The card carries the company, the
fit score, **the one thing** (the single sentence the pitch rests on),
**Share** and a **⋯** menu: *Prep a call*, *What happened?*, *Push to* your
CRM when one is connected, *Write another pitch* and *Download contacts*.
*‹ Library* above it goes back.

- **The pitch** is the sequence: five to seven touches for each named
  contact, email and LinkedIn mixed, each one copyable and pencil-editable.
  The one-pager, the deck and the proposal sit behind the format menu at the
  top of the card, each with what it holds (*11 emails*, *8 slides*).
- **Who to write to** is the decision-makers, with their contacts and, once
  warm paths have been found, a **Way in** column naming who in your network
  reaches them. The warm paths themselves are the card under the table.
- **Why them** is the case: the fit thesis, the signals for and against
  (each rated by recency and recurrence), who the company is with every
  source behind one link, the lookalikes, and *Ask the studio*.

If it is coral, you can click it.

### The sequence

A run writes a sequence **per contact**, not one for the company. Each named
decision-maker gets five to seven touches, and the copy differs per person: a
head of operations and a head of marketing at one company care about
different halves of the same argument, so they get different notes rather
than the same note with the name swapped. At most three contacts, the three
your pitch ranks highest.

**The names sit above the touches.** One contact is on screen at a time; press
a name to switch. Under the name is the arc, one pill per touch, saying where
that touch goes and how long after the one before it. The words are under the
arc.

**Some touches are LinkedIn.** A LinkedIn touch has no subject line, and
Prospektor does not send it: the studio has no LinkedIn connector, so a
connection note or a message is copy you paste into LinkedIn yourself. Its
note is written inside LinkedIn's own 300-character limit, so it fits the box
the first time. Email touches are the same: Prospektor writes them, you send
them.

**Download CSV** on the sequence panel gives you the whole thing as a file,
one row per touch, with the columns Instantly, Apollo and Smartlead already
recognise (`email`, `first_name`, `company`, `step`, `subject`, `body` and
the rest). Import it into whatever you already send with and the mapping step
is usually a confirmation. Anything you have filled into a `[bracketed]`
blank is filled in the file too.

A sequence that covers two of three named contacts says so above the touches.
Press the sequence's own press button again if you want the missing one.

**A run writes the sequence, and leaves the rest to you.** The deck, the
one-pager and the proposal each wait in the format menu with a press button,
one call, under 90 seconds, whenever a pitch turns out to want one. Nothing
is missing and nothing is slower to get; the run simply stops writing three
documents in advance for every company you look at. Decision-makers always
come with the run, because the research call writes them as it goes.
Lookalikes come with a run that scores 50 or better: a lookalike is a company
that fits for the same reasons this one does, so a weak or not-a-fit target
has none, and the card says so rather than listing the target's competitors.

A lookalike row is a name, a similarity and one line on the resemblance;
never a profile. The run researched the target, not them, so nothing on the
row about the company itself comes from memory; where the name was read (the
target's own comparison page, a competitor list) the row links that page in
one word. Press **Glance** on the row to read the company itself.

The card at the top is one look, on purpose: the score and name, and **the
one thing**. Everything else the studio worked out (the firm in a paragraph,
what the run drew on from your workspace, the identity check and the
sources) is the **About** card under *Why them*.

The Fit thesis reads the same way: each bullet of the case and each risk is
one line you can scan, and the objection you will hear comes with a counter
of a few complete sentences you could say back verbatim. Every line ends
properly: the studio rewrites for shortness rather than clipping, so
nothing trails off mid-sentence. The prose version, the argument in full,
sits behind **The full argument**, one press away on the same card.

**The first deck asks one question.** The first time anyone in the workspace
presses *Pitch deck* on a run, the card asks what your decks should be built
from, with three answers. **Write a standing deck** drafts one from your brief
in about half a minute and then builds this company's deck from it. **Upload a
reference** does the same from a deck you already send: pick the .pptx (or a
.txt or .md), the studio reads the slides' text in your browser and keeps the
order and register, and the file itself never leaves your machine. **No
template** writes this deck on its own, one call, and every deck after it the
same way. Whatever you answer is remembered, so the question is asked once;
[Workspace settings](/settings/workspace) → *Deliverables* → *Standing deck* is
where the answer is changed. Only an admin or the owner is asked, because the
answer changes every deck the workspace sends.

**The deck is your standing deck, plus one slide.** Once the workspace has a
standing deck, a pitch does not write one: it reuses those slides, drops in a
slide about this company right after the opening one, and fills your prospect's
name and business into the gaps the template left. That is instant and costs
no call. A workspace that answered *No template* still gets a deck the old way,
pressed in the format menu.

Three deliverables carry their own shape. The **pitch deck** is real slides:
**Download .pptx** on the deck writes a 16:9 file that opens in Keynote,
PowerPoint and Google Slides, one slide per block, in your workspace's own
colours, with the speaker notes on each notes page and the figures' sources
folded in beside them. It is built in your browser, so nothing about the deck
leaves your browser. Edit a slide with its pencil first and the download carries
the edit. Its last slide ends on one quiet line, **Researched by
Prospektor**, the run's source count and the date it ran, the same mark a
shared pitch carries, on the file that gets forwarded furthest. There is no
switch to remove it. The **one-pager** is a value-driven,
print-ready proposal page: your logo and name up top, *why this matters* to
the reader before *why you* are the right one to do it, proof in one-line
points, and one unmissable call to action; Ctrl/Cmd-P turns it into the
page it already looks like. The **proposal** is the formal document you send
once they are interested (scope, commercials and timeline, ready to
forward).

- **A name appears only when a source supports it**: a page the studio read,
  or a contact vendor's record of who holds the role. A role nobody could be
  named for is asked of the vendors, and stays blank rather than guessed when
  they have nobody at the company in that role. A named person without a
  profile link is looked up the same way; an older pitch gets its profiles
  the next time it is opened.
- **Work emails arrive on their own.** Every named person is looked up with
  the contact vendors the studio has keys for, cheapest first, then a routing
  service that tries eight more, and the
  address lands beside the LinkedIn badge, with what verified it in the tooltip; a catch-all domain is said there too. Where Moltsets found it, the tooltip also carries its A to F grade for the mailbox (A validated, B a past send landed, C catch-all, F no signal; an address it grades D is never shown). No
  address means no vendor had a verified one at the company's own domain;
  an address at a company the person has left is dropped, and so is a shared
  desk like `info@`. Emails are included without a cap; the CSV download
  carries them, a shared link does not. A pitch from before addresses existed
  fills in the first time you open it; give it a few seconds.
- **Phones are one press each, and counted.** A dashed *phone?* beside a
  person's address asks the vendor for their number, by the verified work
  email first, so it is theirs at this company. A number found lands there as
  a tap-to-call link and takes one of your workspace's 25 phone lookups for
  the month; the count left is in the button's tooltip. Nothing found costs
  nothing and reads *no phone*. The CSV carries numbers; a shared link never
  does. No *phone?* at all means the free plan, or a studio whose lookups are
  switched off.
- **Bracketed placeholders** in drafts mark what could not be verified.
  They are marked wherever they appear, and the pencil on any block is where
  you fill one in, which also teaches the studio your wording.
- **Find more** under the researched lists queues more research in the
  background; an empty box is a valid instruction ("look again").
- **One specific person** goes in the same box under Decision-makers: a name
  (*Jane Doe*), a LinkedIn profile URL, or either with a role beside it (*Jane
  Doe, CFO*). That person joins the list as you typed them and their work email
  and profile are looked up, the way a run's people are. Someone already listed
  is not added twice. A role on its own (*head of customer operations*) still
  searches for more people.
- **Compliance findings**: the studio still reads its own draft back for
  banned terms and numbers without provenance, and says what it found in the
  run log and the run-ready email. It is a check on the draft, not a screen
  to work through. When the studio could not read the company's own site, a
  finding says so in the studio's own words (*came back empty* for a site
  drawn in the browser, *the check did not complete*, or *could not open*)
  and counts the pages the draft read for itself. That is a note about the
  studio's reading, never a fact about the company: a site the studio cannot
  draw still has its pricing page, and the pitch does not score the empty
  pages as evidence of anything.
- **The pages are one link.** Every page the run read is behind *All 19
  sources ›* at the foot of the About card under *Why them*, each named by
  what that page established; press one and the page opens.
- **Who this is**, on the About card under *Why them*, is the studio's answer to the
  question everything else rests on, in one line: *"Identified as Matte PR by
  reading 11 of their own pages · 3 similar companies ruled out."* Under it,
  and open, are the same-named companies it checked and decided were **not**
  your target, each with the reason. If a company you have never heard of is
  missing from the ruled-out list and its facts are in the profile instead,
  that is the thing to catch before you send anything.
- **Sometimes it says "read 12 days ago", and that is not a shortcut being
  hidden from you.** Working out who a company is means opening their site and
  reading it, and the answer does not change from one week to the next, so
  once any workspace on Prospektor has established it, the reading is kept and
  handed to the next run against that domain instead of being bought again.
  That is why a run can reach the same conclusions in seconds. When the
  reading is not this run's own, the line says when it *was* made, and the
  pages and ruled-out companies behind it are the ones read that day. Nothing
  older than a month is reused; past that the site is read again from
  scratch. If you want a fresh reading sooner than that, say so to support and
  we will clear it for your target.
- **The studio stops looking once it is sure.** Confirming who a company is
  takes a handful of pages, not a hundred: it opens the site, reads the page
  that names the operator, checks that nobody else trades under the name, and
  stops. It spends the full check only where the answer is genuinely in doubt
  (the site would not open, the name you typed is not the name on the site,
  something claims the company has stopped trading, or another business is
  still in the frame). That is why the line above sometimes says four pages and
  sometimes eleven: it is what the answer actually took, not a quota.
- **The highlighted sentences in a draft were written for this company.** They
  are marked where you read them.
  A sentence counts when it names something the run established about the
  target: its name, brand, legal entity or domain, one of the decision-makers
  the research named, where it is or how big it is. Its industry does not
  count, because *B2B SaaS* describes the target and everyone it competes
  with. Unmarked is not wrong: your own proof and your own offer belong in the
  draft and are not about the reader. A draft with nothing marked reads as
  something you could send to anyone. On a shared link the recipient sees the
  count and the highlighting.
- **From your own workspace**, on the About card under *Why them*, says what this run had of
  yours to read: how many recorded outcomes and how many saved edits went
  into the draft. Everything else came from your brief and the live web. A
  run that found no outcomes says so, and offers the door to record one;
  that is the loop that makes a later run better than this one.

## Editing, and what it teaches

The pencil on any deliverable block edits it in place. **Saved edits become
brand-voice examples for future runs**: tone and structure only, never
facts, and facts never cross companies. Nothing else a team does in the
studio teaches it as much.

Since 23 Aug 2026 a run chooses those examples **for the company it is
working on** rather than simply taking the three most recent: the ones whose
subject looks most like this target, with at least one example of each
deliverable the run has to write. So a workspace with fifty saved edits
draws on all fifty, a few at a time, instead of on whichever three were
saved last.

Since 25 Aug 2026 the save also records **how long the block was open** before
you pressed it. That is the studio measuring itself, not you: a draft you had to
spend four minutes fixing was a worse draft than one you fixed in twenty
seconds, and that is the only way this product can honestly tell whether a
change to how it writes actually helped. The record is a duration and the kind
of deliverable, with no address on it and nothing you typed; only Prospektor's
operator sees it, as a median across many runs, and nobody in your workspace or
the agency above it ever does. [Privacy](/help/privacy) says it in full, and a
browser sending Global Privacy Control switches it off while your edit saves
exactly as it would have.

A run also carries what your team recorded in [Outcomes](/outcomes): what
actually won and lost, in their words. The waiting line says so while the
run works: *"Brief loaded, with 4 of your edits as voice references and what
you recorded about 6 companies."* It shapes the judgment, never the copy; a
company from your own outcomes record appearing in a deliverable is flagged by
the compliance check like a banned word is.

## Ask the studio

The last card under *Why them* is a conversation about the pitch: where a claim
came from, how to open the first call, what to say when the predicted
objection lands. It answers only from that pitch and your brief, and never
changes the pitch. Each member has their own conversation per pitch; it
survives reloads.

Questions come out of a daily allowance that every typed-sentence door shares:
this card, the support chat, the home box, the agent builder and *Make sense of
this*. It is roomy on a paid workspace and smaller on a free one, and when it is
spent the studio says so in one line and answers again tomorrow.

## Print / PDF

Ctrl/Cmd-P prints the deliverable styled with your workspace's own stylesheet
(Save as PDF in the same dialog is the PDF export). A deck prints as a deck:
one slide to a landscape sheet. For a file you can present from and edit, use
**Download .pptx** on the deck (the format menu, then *Pitch deck*) instead.

There is no Print / PDF button: it duplicated a keystroke your browser already
has, on a screen that reads better without it.
