# Sharing a pitch

**Share this pitch** on a finished pitch's Summary sends the whole thing;
**Share** on a single deliverable's tab sends just that document. Either
mints a short `/p/<token>` link.

- A full share carries the whole run (fit score, signals, decision-makers,
  lookalikes, every deliverable) styled with your workspace's stylesheet.
  That is your prospecting on a named company: forwarding the link outside
  your team hands it over.
- Narrowing a share to one deliverable sends the document and **none of the
  research**.
- The recipient meets a **gate first**: who sent it, what company it is
  about, and a sign-up. The content is not in the page until an account
  exists. Any signed-in account can read it, but **a share grants sight of
  one pitch, never entry to your workspace**.
- The **Sharing** card on [Workspace settings](/settings/workspace) lists
  every link the team has sent, who opened it
  and when. **Revoke** is one click and works immediately, including for
  someone who already read it. **A link is yours to revoke if you minted it**;
  pulling a colleague's link needs the owner or admin role, because it goes
  dead in the recipient's hands and nothing tells the person who sent it.
  (See [Workspace settings](/help/workspace) for what the roles are.)
- **If the workspace is paused, every link it has sent pauses with it.**
  Anyone opening one is told it is temporarily unavailable, not that it was
  taken back, and nothing about why. No work, no research and no stylesheet
  is served while the workspace is locked, and every link that was not
  revoked comes back the moment the workspace does. Revoking still works
  from the locked screen's side of the wall; a paused link is not a dead
  one, and killing it for good is the one thing a locked workspace still
  lets you do.
- **A share link is not findable in search.** The gate already kept the work
  itself out of the page until an account exists, and the studio now tells
  search engines to keep the whole of `studio.prospektor.ai` (the gate
  included) out of their index. A link is private because you only sent it to
  the people you sent it to; nothing puts it in front of anyone else.
- Every shared pitch ends with one line, **Researched by Prospektor**, the
  run's source count, the date it ran. It is the only mark that survives
  printing (Ctrl/Cmd-P), and there is no switch to remove it. A downloaded
  `.pptx` ends on the same line, on its last slide.
- Speaker notes, compliance findings and the research log never travel on a
  share.

# Your network, and warm paths

A pitch ends with decision-makers to approach cold; the warmer question is
who your team already knows who could open the door.

## Importing your network

[Your network](/network) (the second view of Warm intros on the sidebar) takes the knowledge as
data, without any integration. The first time you open [Warm intro](/intro) with nothing
imported, the same paste box is the whole screen and there are no tabs yet: who you know,
one per line, and **Add them**; the list lands here as *People I know*, and the two views
appear, **Introductions** (the ones to pursue) and **Your network** (the people who make
them). Under the tabs, your network as four totals: people, companies, strong ties and the
last import; without a message tally the line under strong ties offers the tally. Then
**Who introduces you** (below), then **Imports**, one row per import. **Add people ›** on
that card opens the same paste box, with the file imports as quiet links under it (they are
open on their own while nothing is imported), and the small ⓘ by *Imports* holds the fine
print:

- **A pasted list**: one per line, who, then how you know them, after a comma or
  a dash. A minute of typing, no file needed. Press **Add them**. The list is
  called *People I know*; click the name on its row to rename it.

  **Your own colleagues are worth a list of their own.** Every other name is
  somebody outside your company; your colleagues are the one group you can ask
  for an introduction with no favour owed, and their networks are usually the
  largest reach a workspace has. If only some of your team have imported their
  own LinkedIn connections, a pasted list of the rest (names, roles, and a
  profile link after the comma or dash if you have one) covers everyone else
  without asking them to upload anything.
- **A LinkedIn export, per member** (*Import a LinkedIn export*): from
  LinkedIn, Settings & Privacy → Data privacy → "Get a copy of your data" →
  tick Connections → Request archive; LinkedIn emails the `Connections.csv`
  within ~10 minutes, and it uploads here. Re-uploading merges rather than
  double-counting: a connection you already hold is updated in what the new
  export says and keeps its message tally, a new one is added, and one
  LinkedIn has since dropped stays until you remove the import. An import
  older than six months shows **Refresh** on its row, which opens this door.
  **Email addresses in the export are dropped at import and never stored**;
  the studio keeps who and where, never how to email a stranger.
- **An email address book, per member** (*Import an address book*),
  with instructions per provider:
  - **Google (Gmail / Google Workspace)**: contacts.google.com → Export (in
    the left sidebar) → Google CSV, then upload the file here.
  - **Outlook / Office 365**: outlook.office.com/people → Manage contacts →
    Export contacts → all contacts → Export, then upload the file here.

  What is kept per contact: name, company, job title. **Email addresses,
  phone numbers and everything else in the file are dropped at import and
  never stored.** Re-uploading replaces your previous address book import.
- **A message tally, per member** (*Rank them by how well you actually know
  them*, folded into the LinkedIn door): request the same archive again with
  **Messages** ticked, and upload the `messages.csv`. What is kept per person
  is four facts: how many messages you sent them, how many came back, and the
  dates of the first and the last. **No message text, no subjects and no
  thread titles are ever read**, the same rule the address columns get. Import
  your connections first: the tally is added to them rather than stored on its
  own, so removing that import removes the tally with it.
- **Who engaged with a post** (*Paste who engaged with a post*): say what
  the post was in a few words, then paste the names off the reactions panel
  or the comment thread, as LinkedIn shows them. Nothing is fetched from
  LinkedIn. Kept per person: name, role, company, and what they reacted to or
  wrote. The post is the list's name on its row. When somebody at a company
  you then pitch is on that list, the pitch's opener says what they reacted
  to, and the Warm paths panel names them.
- **The people at customers you won** (no door of its own): when the owner
  brings in the won deals from the connected CRM on [Outcomes](/outcomes),
  the people the CRM lists on each deal land here as one list per CRM, *Customers
  in Close* or whichever it is. Kept per person: name, job title, the company and
  the day the deal was won. The CRM's email addresses and phone numbers are not
  read. A customer's staff can vouch for you, so the search names one as the door
  when the company you want is somewhere they can reach.
- **A written `## Network` section** in the brief, for ties that read
  better as prose.

## Who introduces you

Not everyone you know will make an introduction, and a few people will make one
to anyone you ask. The list under the numbers is where you say which is which:
the people from your pasted lists, the people at customers you won, and your
strongest LinkedIn ties, each with two chips, **Always introduces** and **Might
introduce**. One press marks a person, a second press on the lit chip clears it,
and the mark is kept on the import, so removing the import removes it. People
you have marked are listed first. Somebody from a LinkedIn export who is not on
the list is one paste away: type their name into the box and they appear with
the chips.

The mark changes the order everywhere: *Introductions to pursue* and the instant
answer say *will always introduce* beside a marked person, the path finder is
told the team's word outranks any message tally, and the machine surface's
`who_do_we_know` and `list_doors` carry it beside the tie's strength.

Every import is attributed to the member who brought it, and only that
member can remove it. Importing calls no model, and nothing network-shaped
ever travels on a shared link.

## Warm paths

**A tally changes the order, which is the point of adding one.** Without it
the studio ranks your LinkedIn half by how many people you know at a company,
so forty people you have never spoken to outrank the one who actually replies
to you. With it, three rules apply. Someone who wrote to you and never got an
answer scores **zero**; that is how newsletters and cold sequences stay out
of your warm paths. Group threads do not count towards anyone. And a
connection nobody ever messaged is weak by default, but still ranks above
one-way traffic, because a connection is a connection.

With a network in the workspace, every finished pitch gains a **Warm paths**
card under *Who to write to*, and the people table there a **Way in** column
naming who reaches each of them: ranked *you → connector → target* paths, each connector actually in
your network, each claim evidenced with the page it was read on (or the line
of your own data that states it). An honest "checked these, found nothing" is
a normal result.

Asking twice for the same company, or on the same pitch, while a search is
still running gets you that search rather than a second one. A workspace can
start 30 searches a day, and an agency and the client workspaces it created
share 100; past that, the studio asks you to come back tomorrow.

### The best path comes with two drafts, not one

The hard part of an introduction is that saying yes means writing something,
and your connector has ten minutes.

So the panel drafts both halves:

- **The ask**: under 100 words, in your voice, for you to forward to your
  connector: how you know them, one specific low-commitment request, and an
  easy way for them to say no.
- **The email they send on**: under 100 words, in *their* voice, addressed to
  the target and finished. Your connector can send it as it stands, change a
  line first, or ignore it.

Each has its own **Copy**, and the ask has **Open in Mail** as well: it opens
your own mail app with the subject and the text filled in and no address,
because the studio holds none. Anything the studio does not know is left in
[brackets] for whoever fills it in, including in the second draft, because a
guess written in somebody else's voice is not honest.

Under the drafts, four chips say where the introduction stands: **Asked**,
**They said yes**, **No**, **Meeting booked**. A press records it on the
search (or on the pitch), a second press clears it, and *Meeting booked* opens
[Outcomes](/outcomes) with the company filled in, because a meeting is an
outcome worth recording.

**The studio still contacts nobody.** Both drafts are text on your screen. No
mailbox is connected, nothing is sent, and your connector's address is not
something the studio holds.

It runs by itself after a pitch run that scores 50 or better when the workspace
has a network (a warm path is a way in, and below that line the pitch has just
said not to go in) and on demand from the panel (**Find warm paths** / **Look
again**) for any pitch, including one below the line or one that predates an
import. A search is sized to your network: one check per connector, and it
answers within about three minutes with whatever it established.

## If an agency runs your workspace

A workspace an agency set up also reads **their** network when it looks for a
warm introduction. The people listed under a company are the ones who work
there, found by its name, each marked as theirs (*"via Moderne Ventures,
your agency"*) with their role and how strong the tie is. The search also
reads the names and roles on the agency's lists, so a path it finds can run
through one of their contacts who works somewhere else, such as an investor
who knows the founder, and that person is named on the path. Any path through
the agency's people is written as running through the agency, because that
is who would make the introduction. You can't browse or export their list,
and you never see their notes or the profile links. The search never reads
their notes or message counts either.

Nothing is copied. Their imports stay theirs: the member who brought one can
remove it, and removing it takes it out of every workspace at once. Detaching
from the agency ends the reading immediately.

**If you are the agency:** the client workspaces you created read your imports
the same way, and *Your network* says so. One import is enough for a whole
portfolio; there is no need to upload the same export into every workspace.

## Connection-degree chips

The *Everyone at ⟨company⟩* line above the decision-makers carries **1st · 2nd · 3rd+** chips: LinkedIn
people-search links pre-filtered by degree. They open in your own logged-in
LinkedIn, so the degrees are yours; a teammate clicking the same chips sees
their own network. The studio never reads LinkedIn; it only writes search
URLs.

# Inbound: the reply to send, and preparing a call

## Reply: paste what they sent

[Inbound](/evaluate) on the sidebar has two tabs, **Reply** and **Prepare a
call**, and opens on Reply: one box. Paste what a lead sent you, the email,
the LinkedIn message, the form submission, as it is, and press **Write the
reply**. **More options** beside the press opens two optional fields: their
company, if you can tell, and anything the reply must say: your price, when
you can start, what you will not do. That note is the only place a number in the
reply can come from. The studio never invents a price, a date or a promise.

A minute later you get **the reply**, written in your workspace's voice from
the emails you have saved, ready to copy and paste. A lead asking for a quote
gets the two or three questions a quote needs and a line on when they will
have it. A good fit gets the call proposed and what it is for. Somebody
selling gets a short, kind no. One line above the reply says whether they are
worth your time and what the lead is worth; a pill says what the reply does:
quotes your price, asks before quoting, proposes the call, or says no.

Under the reply: **Ask before you quote**, when a quote needs facts the
message does not hold. Behind *Why*: who the sender turned out to be, what
they are actually asking for once the framing is stripped, the argument from
your own brief, how a deal with them could work and the angle to lead with,
and any red flags. A lead worth a call hands into **Prepare the call** with
the sender and the aim prefilled.

Replies are listed in the *Recent* card under the box, never in the Library,
because a reply is not a pitch. Each row says who wrote, whether they are worth
answering, and when; **Open** shows the reply again.

## Prepare a call

[Prepare a call](/prep), the second tab of Inbound (and on every library
card and every finished pitch), takes the company, then asks the one thing the
studio cannot infer, **which call it is**, as five chips: first call,
discovery, pitch, negotiation, or kickoff. Press **Prep me**. **More options**
holds a website and an optional sentence about the call. It hands back one
sheet: the goal
for exactly that call, how to frame it, three to five grounded talking points,
the questions to ask, the objection they will actually raise with an answer
sayable verbatim, and the ask to end on.

Name a company with a saved pitch and the pitch's research rides along whole,
the sheet lands in under a minute and says what it drew on. A prep is a call
sheet, not a pitch: it never appears in the Library, and it is copyable as
plain text. The *Recent preps* card under the form keeps a morning's sheet
findable before the 3pm call.

# Outcomes: what a pitch turned into

Recording what a pitch turned into is **a press on the lead itself**. Every
Library card and every finished pitch carries a badge: it reads *What
happened?* until you set it, and the state afterwards. Press it and pick: a
stage off a short ladder (found the right contact, had a meeting, closed the
deal) or how it ended (went quiet, not a fit, lost). Nothing to navigate to,
nothing to type twice.

Low friction is the whole design, because this is the record that makes the
studio better and it is the one most easily skipped.

So the studio asks. Two weeks after a pitch is written, if nothing is on record
for that company, Home asks one question under the box: *What happened with
Acme?*, with three answers (talking, went quiet, not a fit). One press puts it
on record. It asks about one pitch a visit, the oldest first, and never by
email.

## Bring in the deals you won

The fastest way to fill this record is the deals you have already won. Open
[Outcomes](/outcomes) with nothing on it and the one button is **Bring in your
won deals**: with a CRM connected it asks one question (which stage, status or
list means won in your CRM), reads every deal there, and puts each one on
record as *Closed the deal* with the notes your team kept on it. With no CRM
connected the button is **Connect your CRM**, and takes you to Connectors.
**Or add them yourself** opens the box below, and **Upload a list of won
deals** takes a file: the company, its website, and what happened, one deal per
line. A header row names the columns (company, website, notes), so an export
out of a CRM works as it is and the columns can sit in any order. When a file
has both a *Name* column and a *Company* or *Account* column, the company
column is read, and a list of people (first and last names) is not read as
companies. Once
anything is on record the button is one line above the box.

What comes across, and what does not:

- **Each won deal becomes an outcome record**, the same record you would have
  typed. The stage is *Closed the deal*. The deal's own facts (its name, the
  amount, the day it was won, the stage) are one note, and each note your team
  wrote on the deal in the CRM is a note here, marked where it came from.
- **Every won deal joins your customer list** on Do not contact, so no run is
  ever spent pitching a company you already sell to.
- **Reading it again updates.** A deal already on record is not closed twice
  and a note already here is not copied twice. New notes since last time land.
- **Your word wins.** A company you recorded as closed and then lost stays as
  you left it; the CRM's notes still land beside it.
- **Nothing is written into your CRM** by a read, and nothing is sent to a
  model by it. *Make sense of this* on any record is still a press of yours.
- **Which CRMs:** Lightfield and HubSpot, by the stage that means won;
  Close, by the status that means won; Affinity, by a deals list and the
  status value on it. Reevo, Attio and HighLevel cannot be read this way yet.

A read is the workspace owner's, because it uses the CRM key. An upload is
anyone's. Twenty-five deals per read, with the real number said when there
are more; the next read takes the next ones.

**Any company, found here or not.** Open [Outcomes](/outcomes), type the
company, and say what happened: a reply, a meeting, a win, a loss. It does
not have to be a lead the studio found. An inbound call that closed, a
referral, a deal your team brought in themselves: record it, and the next
pitch is written with it in mind. The screen asks one thing at a time. The
company box first; once it holds a name, one row of six chips asks what
happened, with the chip for where the company stands today already marked,
so picking another one records a move. The note box under it takes their
reply, your notes or a transcript as they are, and one **Save it** records
all of it. Every company on record is listed below; press a row to open it.

- The record is per **company**, not per pitch: an inbound deal that closed
  without a run still gets a record, and two runs on one target are one
  relationship.
- **Notes and the full history** live at [the outcome record](/outcomes):
  free text taken verbatim (call notes, a pasted email thread, "they bought
  because the CFO wanted the one-pager"), the timeline of every move, and the
  studio's own reading. Open it with **Add a note…** on any card's badge.
- **Make sense of this** has the studio read the whole record back and
  propose, beside the notes, what actually won or lost this one, anchored
  in the notes' own words, and the few follow-up questions worth answering
  next. It never changes the record; **Look again** is the update story.
- **What next?**, since 10 Sep 2026, the forward half. Paste what came back
  (their reply, your notes from the meeting, a transcript) into the same
  box, and the button reads **Save and say what's next**: one press saves it
  and has the studio answer with where the deal now stands (one tap to mark
  it), the one next step and the line in the material that decides it, the
  message that step needs written in your voice and ready to copy, and a
  short checklist of what is owed that you tick as you go. It replaces *Make
  sense of this* while a deal is live and hands back to it once the deal has
  closed or ended. A suggestion beside your notes, never a change to them;
  nothing is sent anywhere, and no mailbox is read; you paste, on purpose.
  **Again** re-reads after the next paste and keeps your ticks.
- Companies recorded as **closed** feed the Leads shelf's next refill as
  its strongest evidence, so what the shelf offers drifts toward what
  actually closes.
- **And since 23 Aug 2026, what you record shapes what the studio writes.**
  A bounded digest of your own record (where each prospect got to, how it
  ended, the studio's reading of it where you asked for one, and your team's
  newest notes in their own words) now rides every pitch run, every call
  prep and every inbound evaluation. Wins and losses both: a deal that died
  on implementation time teaches the next draft as much as one that closed.
  The records closest to the company being worked on go first, and the
  record for that exact company always travels when you have one.
- It stays inside the studio. The studio is told, in the prompt itself, that
  nothing from your outcomes goes into a deliverable (not a quote, not a
  number, not the name of another company you have been talking to) and that
  nothing there is to be looked up on the web. And because an instruction is
  not a guarantee, the same check that reads every draft back for banned words
  now also flags any company from your own outcomes record that turns up in
  the copy, next to the block it turned up in. Your pipeline steers the
  writing; it is not material to send.
- So the studio does get better the more you use it, and outcomes are the
  loop that makes that true. A workspace that has recorded fifty deals runs
  differently from one opened this morning.
- **And since 24 Aug 2026 the product says so where you can see it.** The
  outcome record opens by stating what recording does rather than only how
  to file it, the note box says that what you write is what the next run
  reads, and every finished pitch carries **From your own workspace** on its
  Summary (behind *The full picture*): how many recorded outcomes and how many saved edits that draft was
  written with. When the answer is none, it says that too, and offers the way
  to fix it. It is your own count, on your own screen; a shared link never
  carries it.
- **And since 26 Aug 2026 the studio tells you once when the loop starts
  turning.** The first time three or more companies are on your record with
  something readable on them, whoever recorded that third one gets a single
  email (*the studio is starting to write like you*) naming the companies it
  read and where each one stands, plus how many more are on record than any one
  run reads. If you have also saved an edited deliverable it says how many of
  your edits are being read back as voice references; if you have not, it says
  that instead, because that is the half of the loop still missing. It is sent
  **once in the life of a workspace** and never again, it goes only to the
  person who recorded the outcome, it never repeats your notes back at you, and
  it can be switched off in advance from
  [Workspace settings](/help/workspace) like any other mail about your work.

## Remove a company recorded by mistake

Open the company's record from [Outcomes](/outcomes) and press **Remove this
record** under its timeline. The record goes, notes included, and the studio
stops using it: no row on Leads for you, no paid search for companies like
it, nothing about it in the next pitch, prep or evaluation. It asks first,
because there is no undo. A record a colleague has written on can be removed
by the workspace's owner or an admin.

A won deal your CRM still reports comes back the next time you bring in your
won deals. Fix that one in the CRM. Removing the record does not take the
company off your customer list on Do not contact.

## What the studio would write differently now

Recording outcomes makes the next run better, and until now you only got that
benefit on the companies you happened to run again. The screen now says which
ones those are.

A company appears here when two things are true: you recorded it as having
gone quiet or been lost, and you have taught the studio at least three things
since that day. Those three can be outcomes you recorded on other companies or
deliverables you edited and saved, because both ride every run. The line says
which, and how many.

The claim is deliberately narrow. It says a pitch written today would be
**different**, not that it would be better, because different is what the
record can prove and better is what your own judgment decides. Press **Pitch
again** and the company goes into a fresh run with everything you have recorded
since. Nothing starts on its own; a run costs money and the press is yours.

A company you marked **not a fit** never appears here. That was your judgment
about the company rather than about the argument, and a fresh pitch is not the
remedy for it.

**And once a week it can come to you instead.** The same list arrives as an
email, at most weekly, and only in a week where something has actually gone
stale. A quiet week sends nothing at all. It goes to everyone on the workspace,
because any of you can act on it, and it carries a company name, how it ended
and two counts: it never repeats your notes back at you. Turn it off from
[Workspace settings](/help/workspace) like any other mail about your work, or
leave it on and keep using the screen. This one is off for everybody until we
switch it on.

## Why you win and why you lose

Each record says what happened with one company. This reads all of them at
once, the deals you won and the deals you lost, and looks for the reason that
repeats: the argument that keeps winning, and the one that keeps losing.

Once enough of your won or lost deals have notes on them, the
[Outcomes](/outcomes) screen offers **Read why you win and lose**. One press
reads them and comes back with a few findings at most. Each one names the
deals it was read from, and a reason only one deal shows is never offered,
because one lost deal is an anecdote.

Nothing changes until you say so. Press **Keep** and the line goes into your
brief, where every pitch, prep and evaluation reads it from then on: lean on
what wins, and stop making the argument that loses. Press **×** on a kept line
to take it off your brief again, or on a finding you disagree with to dismiss
it. A line never names one of your companies, and it is never quoted into a
deliverable.

Press **Read again** after you have recorded more. What you kept stays kept.

## Bring your call recordings

A notetaker already wrote your calls down, and those transcripts teach the
brief the same way your won and lost deals do.

Export them from Fathom, Otter, Granola, Zoom or whatever records your calls,
then press **Bring your call recordings** on the [Outcomes](/outcomes) screen
and pick up to six. Each call is read on its own for three things: the
objections the other side raised, the questions they asked, and the answers
that visibly landed.

What comes back is the list above, with the same **Keep** and the same **×**, so
a line reaches your brief only when you say so. Each line names the calls it was
read from, and one that two calls both produced comes first: an objection you
hear twice is the one worth answering before it is raised.

Your transcript is read once and thrown away. What stays is the handful of
sentences the read wrote, and the file's name. Timestamps, links and email
addresses come out before the call is read at all, and a line that quotes a
phone number, a web address or a company you already have on record is never
proposed.

Each file counts as one of your day's reads, so six files is six.

There is no minimum here. This works in your first week, before any deal has
ended, which is the one thing the read above cannot do.

Drop a `.txt`, `.md`, `.vtt` or `.srt` file. A PDF or a Word document will not
be read, so export as text, and a file with only a few words in it is named back
to you rather than read.

# Your brief, your account, and the workspace

Since the settings page was split, three screens do what one used to:
[Your brief](/settings/brief) (`/settings/brief`), [Your
account](/settings/account) (`/settings/account`) and [Workspace
settings](/settings/workspace) (`/settings/workspace`). The split is by owner:
the brief is the workspace's working document, the account is yours and follows
you between workspaces, and the rest is administration. `/settings` is the
Settings page: four cards of rows, one per page. Every page a row opens has the
same shape: its title, then its settings in white cards, each a title and a
few rows.

## The brief

[Your brief](/settings/brief) holds the brief: the facts, voice,
guardrails and banned terms every pitch is drafted against, plus what the
studio has learned from your team's edits. The studio writes to the brief
while it is still researching a new workspace; **saving the brief yourself
takes it over for good**: the studio stops writing to it, and later
research is dropped rather than merged over a human's corrections.

**It reads as one document.** *Who you are*, *What you charge*, *How you
sound*, *What has worked*, *Never*, each as its first three lines with a count that opens the
rest. A question the studio still has is a blank line in the section its
answer belongs in: press it, answer, and the answer lands in your brief in your
own words. **Edit** is the one button, and it opens the markdown, which is the
moment saving takes the brief over. The studio's own draft notice stays in the
file, where Edit shows it.

**What you charge** is your price list, read off your own pricing page, with
the day it was read. Every pitch, call sheet and glance is written knowing it.
Prices change, so the studio reads the page again after 90 days, unless you
have edited the brief: then the list is yours, and Edit is how you correct it.

Under the document, *Rescan your site*, folded: open it for the one press.
What the studio has learned from your team's work is on
[Outcomes](/outcomes), not here.

**If your goal arrived after the research.** The studio asks what you are
hunting for the moment the workspace exists, and it spends minutes reading your
site. When your answer lands after that reading, the goal at the top of your
brief is yours and the thinking underneath it was written without it. The fold
at the foot of your brief opens itself to say so and offers **Rescan the
site**, which re-reasons the whole brief with your goal and writes nothing
until you accept it.

## Your standing deck

A pitch deck is mostly about *you*: what you do, the proof it works, how an
engagement runs, the ask. Those slides do not change from one prospect to the
next, so the studio writes them **once** for the workspace instead of inventing
them again for every company you look at.

**It is asked for at the first deck, not here.** The first time an admin
presses *Pitch deck* on a run, the tab asks whether to write a standing deck
from the brief, build one from a deck you already send (*Upload a reference*),
or use no template. Six to eight slides, one call, about half a minute. Read it
under *Standing deck* on [Workspace settings](/settings/workspace) →
*Deliverables*, fix any slide with its pencil, and it is saved for good; the
deck a pitch shows is the deck you approved, not one a model wrote while you
were not looking. That block is where the answer is changed: a workspace that
said *No template* can write or upload one there, and *Replace or remove* under
a written deck does what it says. Writing or replacing it needs the admin or
owner role, because every deck the workspace sends after it is built from those
slides; anyone in the workspace can read it.

**What each pitch adds is one slide.** The studio inserts a slide about that
company (the one thing the pitch rests on, the evidence behind it, and what
they will say back in the speaker notes) straight after your opening slide, and
fills in your prospect's name and business wherever a slide left a gap for
them. Nothing else about the deck is rewritten, and no separate call is made to
build it, so a deck now appears the moment you open its tab.

Three gaps a slide can leave for the studio to fill: `[company]`,
`[what they do]` and `[the wedge]`. Anything else you leave in brackets stays in
brackets (the studio's mark for a word it did not write) for you to fill
before you send.

**Remove it** and every pitch goes back to writing its own deck from scratch,
one call at a time. **Write it again** replaces it, and loses your edits to it.

**Two lines in the brief are not yours to type.** Who can sign in
(`allowedEmails:`) is set in Workspace settings, and how the workspace pays
(`plan:`) is set by how it was created. Edit either and the save still
succeeds; the line is simply rewritten back to what is true.

**Three parts of the brief the editor does not own.** The brief is a text box
every member of the workspace can reach, so the lines that decide what the
workspace is *allowed to do* (and anything nobody else should read) are not
one edit away from anybody who can type:

- **`allowedEmails`**: who can sign in. Changed on the access list in
  [Workspace settings](/settings/workspace) → *Workspace*, never by
  typing in the brief: an edit that changes those lines saves everything else
  and leaves the list where it was.
- **`agency`**: whether this workspace may create client workspaces of its
  own. That is your plan, and only Prospektor sets it (a workspace whose brief
  is a committed file says it in the file). An edit that adds the line saves
  everything else and quietly drops it, so the brief never claims a plan the
  workspace does not have.
- **`integrations`**: a CRM or enrichment slot names a provider, and nothing
  else. **API keys do not go in the brief**: everyone who can open this page
  could read one. A save that types a key is refused and says so; name the
  provider here, and the key is asked for by the integration that needs it.

## Saying no: Do not contact

Everything else in the studio is a way of asking it to find companies.
[Do not contact](/suppress), a page of Settings, is the one place that tells it
who **not** to. It has two halves, and most workspaces need both.

### The standing rules

One disqualifier per line, in your own words:

```
Mostly remote workforce
No public-facing brand
Anyone already using a competing platform
```

The box offers that example, marked *For example*, until you save something of
your own. A saved rule is your own text, in ink; the example is grey and says
so. The two can never be confused.

These go into your brief, so they are checked everywhere the studio decides
who is worth approaching: the Leads shelf, its refills, and the fit score
on every run. A rule outranks a good score on every other dimension: where a
target meets one, the pitch says so in its first line and scores the company
down rather than talking itself round.

This is the half that keeps working on companies nobody has named yet, which
is why it is worth writing even if your list is empty.

### Never them: the named list

**Add a company or person** opens the form: a name, a reason and one line of
context. **A customer you name in the box above is added for you**, as a
customer, the moment you save, and so is a card you mark *Our client* on For
you. So is every customer your own site names with a quote, a title or a case
study: the studio reads them while it drafts your brief and adds each one with
the note *Named as a customer on* your site, so it never proposes a company
you already have. Most teams add the other two by hand: **our own
competitors** and **anyone who asked us to stop**.

- A **company** entry is enforced before anything is spent. Starting a pitch
  against it is refused, a Beast Mode batch skips that row and says why, and
  the company never reaches the Leads shelf, including a card that was
  already sitting there before you added the entry. A run you already have
  keeps its card in the Library, marked with the reason (*Your customer*)
  where its score stood, and sorted last.
- A **person** entry never blocks their employer. One person saying no is not
  their company saying it, so the pitch still runs; the studio is told not to
  name them as a decision-maker, address a draft to them or route an
  introduction through them, and if their name appears in the finished draft
  anyway the pitch carries a blocker saying so.
- Adding a company that is **already on the list** updates the reason and the
  note, and keeps the original attribution: who first said no is the fact
  worth keeping.

A website is worth adding on a company entry. Names get typed differently
("Acme", "Acme Ltd", "Acme Logistics") and the domain is what matches without
anyone having to guess the spelling. Company names match with the legal form
stripped, so *Acme Ltd* and *Acme* are the same entry.

A LinkedIn profile is worth adding on a person entry, for the same reason.
People change their names, and the profile is what keeps them on the list when
they do. With one on the entry, the studio holds the person back when it meets
either their name or their profile. The profile is kept with the entry and goes
when the entry goes.

The company box suggests as you type: pick a company and the website box fills
itself, which is the fastest way to get an entry that actually matches. It goes
quiet while you are adding a person; a colleague's name is not a company, and
the studio never sends one anywhere to look it up.

### Who added it, and taking one off

Every entry records who added it and when, and the screen shows both. So does
the refusal when somebody tries to run a pitch against it; the person meeting
the rule is usually not the person who wrote it, and lifting it is a decision
they can only make knowing whose decision they are reversing.

Anyone in the workspace can remove an entry. The exception is an entry whose
reason is **asked not to be approached**: that record is the studio's own
proof the request was honoured, so removing it takes a second confirmation.
Removing it does not un-send anything; it only means nothing stops the next
pitch.

**This is not the same as the "ruled out" companies on a finished pitch.**
Those are the studio's own working-out (same name, different company) shown
so you can check which business it actually researched. The suppress list is
your instruction, and the studio obeys it without arguing.

### If saving your rules is refused

Your rules are kept in two places that have to agree: your workspace's record,
and the `negativeCriteria:` block in your brief's frontmatter. The brief is
what every run and every suggestion is actually scored against, so if the
studio cannot write your rules into it, it will not tell you they were saved
but refuses the save and says which part of the brief it could not edit.

That normally means the brief's frontmatter has been hand-edited into a shape
the studio cannot safely rewrite, most often the same key written twice. Open
the [brief editor](/brief), fix the `negativeCriteria:` block so it appears
once, and save your rules again. Nothing is lost in the meantime: until the
save succeeds, the rules already in force stay in force.

### If your brief lives in the repository

A workspace whose brief is a committed file is edited there and deployed, so
the standing rules are read-only on this screen. The named list still works
normally: it is stored per workspace, not in the brief.

## Affiliate: refer a workspace

**Affiliate**, under Settings › Personal, is one sentence: refer a workspace
and earn 20% of what it pays, for twelve months. Until the programme is on it
reads *Coming soon*; once it is, the same card carries the link to the partner
signup. Nothing in the studio counts a commission or makes a link: the
programme runs on the partner platform, and the terms are on
[prospektor.ai/partners](https://prospektor.ai/partners/).

## Appearance: light, dark, or your machine's

**Where it is:** click your workspace's name at the top of the sidebar (the
same menu that holds your other workspaces, Your account and Sign out) and
**Appearance** is at its foot. That is the only place it lives; it used to be
repeated at the bottom of the settings page as well.

The menu stays open while you click, so you can try light against dark with the
studio visible behind it.

Three settings:

- **System** follows whatever this computer is set to, and keeps following
  it. A machine that switches to dark at sunset switches the studio with
  it, with no reload. This is the setting you start on.
- **Light**: always light, whatever the machine says.
- **Dark**: always dark.

Two things worth knowing:

**It follows you, not the workspace.** Your colleagues are not affected, and
neither are your other workspaces; switching between clients never changes
the studio's colour. The choice is saved on the device you set it on and,
while you are signed in, on your account too, so your laptop and your desktop
start the same way and the most recent choice on either wins. A browser in
private mode forgets it when the window closes and picks your account's
choice up again on the next sign-in.

**Deliverables stay on white paper in either theme.** A deck, one-pager,
proposal or email is what your client will be looking at, so it is rendered
the same way in both: a white sheet inside the dark studio. Shared links
are all deliverable, so a share page is always light, whatever the person
reading it has their machine set to. Printing is light for the same reason.

## Your account: how you sign in, and your recovery number

[Your account](/settings/account) (`/settings/account`) is **yours rather than
any workspace's**: it follows you into every workspace you belong to, and your
colleagues each keep their own. Open it as **Profile**, the first row of
Settings, or from the workspace menu at the top of the sidebar.

**How you sign in.** Every passkey on your account, what each one is, when it
was added and when it was last used, with *Add a passkey* to make another and
*Remove* to forget one. A passkey is Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello or a
security key; the secret half never leaves your device and it only ever works
on this site, which is what makes it impossible to phish. Add one per device
you use. Removing one stops it opening the studio; you can still sign in with
Google or an emailed link. Full explanation in
[Getting started](/help/getting-started).

**Recovery phone number.** So we can get you back in if you lose access to
your email, and so there is a way to reach you about the account itself. Pick
your country, then write the number the way you normally would. It is used for
nothing else unless you allow it below (never sent to a model, never in a
deliverable) and you can clear it here whenever you like.

**Emails about your work.** Four switches, all **on from the start**: these are
reports on your own workspace rather than news about us, so nobody is asked
permission for them. Each goes only to the person who started the work, never to
the rest of the workspace.

- *When a run finishes.* A run takes two to five minutes and keeps going whether
  or not you stay on the screen, so when it lands the studio emails you, with
  the fit score, the angle it chose and the opening lines of the draft in the
  mail itself, not just a link.
- *When a batch finishes.* The runs inside a Beast Mode batch are **not** emailed
  one by one; fifty targets would be fifty emails. Instead one mail at the end
  names the companies that scored 75% or higher with their own scores, links to
  each, and says how many of the runs landed. Nothing over 75% is reported too,
  with what the closest actually scored.
- *When fresh suggestions land.* The Leads list refills itself when it runs
  short, and the search lands minutes after the look that fired it, usually
  after you have moved on. A mail names the companies that landed, at most one
  every six hours,
  with their scores where the search scored them, and nothing more: a refill
  that found nothing sends nothing, and neither the opening suggestions you
  watch arrive during setup nor the search their hand-over starts is mailed;
  you are on the screen for both.
- *When the studio starts writing in your voice.* **One email, once in the life
  of a workspace**, the only one here that is not about a piece of work
  finishing. It arrives when three or more companies are on your Outcomes record
  with something on them the studio can actually read, which is the point at
  which what you have written down starts steering every pitch, call prep and
  inbound evaluation after it. It names the companies it read and where each one
  stands, says how many more are on record than one run reads, and tells you
  whether your saved edits are yet teaching it how you write. It never repeats
  your notes back at you; those stay in the record. After it, nothing like it
  is sent again, whatever else you record.

One more is written and switched off for everybody: a weekly note when a pitch
has gone stale against your own record ([what it says](/help/outcomes)). It is
the one mail here that goes to the whole workspace rather than to one person,
because any of you can act on it. It joins this list the day we switch it on.

Any of them can be switched off here, or from the *unsubscribe* link at the foot
of any one of them, whenever you like, one switch at a time, so stopping the
batch mail leaves the run mail alone. Turning one **back on** is done here, never
from a link.

Sign-in links, receipts and service notices come with having an account, so
they are not on that list and cannot be switched off.

If your email provider starts rejecting mail to your address, or one of our
emails is reported as spam, the studio stops sending anything but those sign-in
links and service notices, and this block says so, rather than showing you a
switch nobody touched in the off position.

**How we may reach you.** The four contact permissions, exactly as the first
card asked them: product email, account texts, product texts, phone calls.
Every one is off unless you turned it on, and unticking one here takes it back
straight away. Account email (sign-in links, receipts, service notices) is
not on the list, because it is part of having an account.

Neither of these is deleted when a workspace is: how you sign in to your other
workspaces is not one workspace's to take away.

## What this workspace is called

The name at the top of your brief goes on everything the workspace produces.
If your workspace was created from a checkout, by an agency, or from an
uploaded list, the first owner or admin to sign in is asked once to confirm it.
Confirming rewrites the brief itself, so every pitch afterwards is composed
under the name you agreed to.

To change it later, open **Workspace settings → Workspace → Name**, the
field is there for the workspace's owner and admins,
and saving it rewrites the brief the same way confirming did. Members see the
name and who can change it. There is no need to edit the `name:` line in the
brief editor by hand, and it is better not to: a hand-edited brief is treated
as yours from then on, and the studio stops writing research into it.

## The website this workspace is built on

Everything the studio writes comes from one site: the one it read when the
workspace was created. Renaming a workspace does not change it (the name is a
label, and the site is what the model reads) so a workspace relabelled for a
different company will go on finding companies for the old one.

To point it somewhere else, open **Workspace settings → Workspace
configuration → Website**, type the new address, and press **Change**. The
studio reads the new site and rewrites your brief from it. That takes about a
minute, and the dashboard says so while it runs.

### More than one website

Some companies publish on several addresses, a product site beside a corporate
one, a second-language domain, a brand mid-rebrand. Press **Add another site**,
type it, and press **Change**. The studio reads them all and writes **one**
brief: one set of facts, one voice, one fit thesis, one workspace. Four sites is
the limit.

The first field is the primary: the address the rest of the studio uses, and
the one the shelf and every run resolve to. **✕** removes a site, and **Change**
then reads what is left. Every site is read again on each press, so this is the
same minute of research either way.

**Say it when you create the workspace, not after.** If you already know a
company has two addresses, the agency's **New client workspace** form has the
same **Add another site** button; press it before you create them and the very
first research reads both. Adding the second address afterwards works and costs
you nothing but time: it is another minute of research, on a workspace that has
just spent one.

### Changing companies, not just addresses

The confirmation asks one more thing: whether to **clear what the old site
taught this workspace**. The two cases are different and only you know which
one you are in.

- **Same company, new address.** Leave it unticked. Your saved pitches,
  outcomes, voice examples and setup answers stay, and only the site reading is
  replaced.
- **A different company.** Tick it. Every finished run, saved pitch, voice
  example and your setup answers are deleted, and the brief goes back to a
  blank one the new research fills in. Type the workspace name to confirm.
  There is no undo.

The second one is what to use when a workspace is becoming something else.
Leaving the old work in place is what makes a repointed workspace keep
suggesting the old company's prospects: your setup answers say what to hunt
for, and edited drafts are what the studio learned your voice from.

**Some things survive either way**, and deliberately. Who has access and
everyone's role. Your suppress list, including anyone who asked not to be
approached, which is a record Prospektor does not delete quietly. Networks
your team imported. Your deliverable stylesheet. Your subscription: this
changes the work, never the bill.

**Your workspace keeps its name.** If you have named it yourself, that name
stays; changing the website does not rename anything you decided. If you have
never named it (it is still called whatever was typed at checkout or by the
agency that set it up), clearing lets the studio name it from the new site.
Either way the name is one press away in *Workspace name*, just above.

**Only the workspace's owner can do it.** An admin can rescan the site the
workspace already has, but not change which company it is. If your workspace
is committed to the repository, its website is changed there and deployed.

## The language the studio writes in

Every pitch, deck, email, prep sheet, intro draft and support answer comes out
in one language: English, Spanish, German or Dutch. The studio sets it from
your browser when the workspace is created (or from the language you bought
it in, if you checked out on prospektor.ai in Spanish, German or Dutch) so
most people never touch it.

To change it, open **Workspace settings → Workspace → Language** and press
the one you want. It applies from the next run; nothing already written is
translated.

One case where the press does not take, and the studio tells you so. If you
have edited your brief by hand, the studio stops writing to it, so it records
your answer and leaves the brief alone. Set the language yourself by putting a
`language:` line at the top of the brief, with `en`, `es`, `de` or `nl` after
it. The same is true of **Whose studio this is** just above it.

Three things stay as they are whatever you pick. Company and product names,
people's names and titles, and anything you quote. Your own words in the
brief; the studio never translates what you wrote. And the brief's section
headings, which stay English because the studio reads them by name.

Whichever you pick, the screens follow: every button, label and message in
the studio and on a shared pitch, and the cookie notice with them.

The help you are reading follows too, article by article: one that has not
been translated yet is served in English rather than going missing.

How the studio addresses a reader in what it writes (*usted* or *tú*, *Sie*
or *du*, *u* or *je*) is yours to state under **Brand voice** in your brief;
where you say nothing, it writes formally. The screens address you as *tú*,
*du* and *je*.

**Workspace settings → Connect your apps.** One grid holds every door out of

*Connect*, *Connected*, *Failed*, *Reconnect*. Press one and its panel opens underneath.

Only the workspace's owner sees this section. Each of these acts as the whole
