# Troubleshooting: what things mean

- **The studio keeps finding companies for the wrong business**: usually a
  workspace that was renamed but never repointed. The name is a label; the
  site the studio read is what every run is written from. Change it under
  *Workspace settings → Workspace configuration → Website*, and tick *clear
  what the old site taught it* if this is now a different company; your
  setup answers and learned voice are the other half of what keeps the old
  hunt alive. See [Workspace settings](/help/workspace).
- **Results marked "simulated"**: the deploy has no model key configured;
  the plumbing ran but nothing was researched. On the production studio this
  should never appear; if it does, that is worth reporting.
- **Blank decision-maker names**: deliberate, not a bug. A name is filled
  only when a credible source supports it; blanks are left for your own
  enrichment rather than guessed.
- **Bracketed placeholders in a draft**: facts the studio could not verify
  and refused to invent. They are marked wherever they appear; the pencil on
  the block is where you fill one in before sending.
- **"Sign in with a passkey" does nothing, or says no passkey was used**:
  either you have not made one on this device yet, or you dismissed the
  browser's prompt. Sign in with Google or an emailed link, then add one from
  [Your account](/settings/account). A passkey lives on the
  device that made it: adding one on your laptop does not put one on your
  phone unless your browser syncs them for you.
- **The passkey button is not on the sign-in page**: the browser cannot make
  passkeys. Recent Chrome, Safari, Edge and Firefox all can; a very old
  browser or a locked-down work profile may not. The emailed link works
  everywhere.
- **"This passkey looks like it has been copied"**: the key answered with a
  counter that went backwards, which is what a duplicated security key looks
  like. Remove it in *Your account* and enrol a fresh one; if you did not
  duplicate anything, tell us.
- **"Include the country code"** on the recovery number: a number without one
  cannot be dialled from where support would be dialling it. Write it as
  `+49 176 1234567`.
- **"Nothing here was opened just now"** on a free run: the first step
  described the company from what the model already knew rather than from
  their live site. It is unusual; the glance opens the homepage. When it
  happens the studio says so instead of heading the block *"what we read on
  your site"*, because a guess dressed as a reading is worse than a guess.
  Read what it says with that in mind, and correct the hunting sentence in
  step two if it is off; the companies it goes and finds come from that
  sentence, not from the guess.
- **A scan that stops without answering**: the site took longer than twenty
  seconds to open, and the studio stops waiting rather than hold you on a
  spinner. Ask again in a minute; most sites answer the second time. If the
  glance had already read a page before it ran out, it answers from that page
  and says only what it actually read.
- **"acme.com would not open, so it was not read"**: the site did not answer
  at all: nothing listening, a certificate that never completed, a page that
  refused the reader. The scan says so rather than describing a page it never
  opened, and the domain is asked again an hour later. If the site is up for
  you, try once more after that hour; if it is down, no reading is the right
  answer.
- **"A website, not a name, like competitor.com"**: the field takes an
  address, not a company name: `ueno.co`, `www.ueno.co` and
  `https://ueno.co/work` all work, "Ueno" does not. Every real suffix is
  accepted, `.co` and `.inc` among them.
- **A run that sits on one stage for minutes**: research reads the live
  web and is the long stage; the activity line under it ("2 searches · 9
  sources read") is the sign it is alive. A run has fifteen minutes; one
  that hits that limit is marked *did not finish* on the screen you are
  watching it from, with **Rerun** right there. Everything else the studio
  runs behind a screen keeps the same clock: a competitor report, a call
  prep, an inbound verdict, a **Find more**, a portfolio upload and a site
  rescan all read *did not finish* past fifteen minutes, with the press
  that starts a fresh one beside them. A rescan that was cut off no longer
  blocks the next one; press **Try again**.
- **The research behind your first screen**: it is the one run that starts
  itself again. If it is cut off, or never starts at all, it restarts once
  and says nothing; only a second failure says *"The research did not
  finish, twice"*, and *Rescan your site* at the foot of
  [Your brief](/settings/brief) is the way on from there. Your answers count
  either way; the questions never waited on the research.
- **"The studio's records aren't answering. Reconnecting…"**: the studio
  could not read its records when it opened. It asks again by itself, more
  slowly each time, for six minutes, and the screen appears the moment they
  answer. Nothing to press. Whether it is just you or everyone is one line at
  [prospektor.ai/status](https://prospektor.ai/status/), read fresh every half
  minute and linked from that banner; a **Status** that says *degraded since*
  means we already know.
- **"The studio hit a busy moment"**: the model provider was overloaded.
  The run retries by itself (it says so in its log) before it ever gives
  up; one that fails anyway offers **Rerun** (same target, same ticks, and
  a failed glance reruns as a glance)
  and **Share this bug with Prospektor**, which sends that run's error and
  step log to us for analysis, only on that click. When a shared report leads
  to a fix, the workspace gets one run on us and the Plan card in
  **Settings** says which fix it paid for.
- **"The research call ran longer than the studio allows"**: the research
  step filled its whole budget before it finished. Rare, and **Rerun** is the
  fix: it starts again on the same target and usually lands.
- **"Suggestions could not be loaded"** on the home screen: the line names
  what the studio actually hit, and **Try again** re-asks without reloading.
  If it keeps saying the same thing, Support has the wording it needs.
- **"Drafted from a partial brief"** on a pitch: the run started before
  the workspace's research or interview finished. The pitch is real but
  worth less; sharpening the brief and running again is the fix. A brief you
  have written yourself never carries the label, whatever the research did.
- **"Read from public sources" under your brief**: your own site would not
  open when the studio went to read it, so the brief was assembled from what
  is published about you elsewhere: indexed pages, directories, filings,
  press. It is thinner than a brief read off your own pages, especially the
  voice rules, so it is worth correcting by hand. Sites hosted on Squarespace,
  Wix and similar platforms sometimes refuse automated readers outright. Use
  *Rescan your site* at the foot of [Your brief](/settings/brief) if the site
  has changed since; a rescan that gets in replaces the label.
- **"Your pages come back empty without a browser"**: your site is drawn in
  the browser (a single-page app), and the studio's reader has none, so it
  reads what is public about you instead, the same way as above. A target
  company built that way gets the same treatment: its pitch says so in the
  compliance findings, lists none of those pages as read, and never scores
  the empty pages as evidence about the company. The site is asked again on
  the next run rather than remembered as unreadable.
- **The brief says your site could not be read, while a rescan is running**:
  fixed. The banner reads what is happening now: it says a rescan is in
  flight while one is, and says a reading is waiting once one has landed, with
  a link to it. If you still see a stale failure alongside a running rescan,
  that is worth reporting.
- **A paused workspace**: the subscription behind it lapsed. The lock
  screen's resubscribe button reopens the same studio with everything kept.
  Shared links pause with it and come back with it.
- **"The studio's records aren't answering. Reconnecting…"**: a storage
  outage on our side; nothing is lost, and you do not have to do anything.
  The studio keeps asking and opens by itself the moment the records come
  back, usually inside a few minutes. Only if it is still out after six
  minutes does it stop and offer you a *Try again* button.
- **The sign-in page during an outage**: it loads and works normally. It
  needs none of the records, so a storage outage no longer keeps you off it.
- **Someone can't sign in**: their address is probably not on the
  workspace's allowlist; the owner adds it in [Workspace
  settings](/settings/workspace) → *Access* → *Who has access*.
  Removal takes effect immediately, and so does adding. A storage hiccup is
  never the reason you are told you have no access: those say so in their own
  words, in the reconnecting banner above.
- **A share link stopped working**: it was revoked or expired. Mint a new
  one from the pitch; [Workspace settings](/settings/workspace) → *Sharing*
  shows every link's state.
- **A recipient says a link is "not available right now"**: the workspace
  is paused, so every link it has sent is paused too. Reactivating brings
  them all back; nothing was revoked and nothing was lost.
- **No suggestions on the home screen**: normal for a brand-new workspace
  while research lands, and the shelf refills over time; running pitches
  and recording outcomes are what feed it.
- **A portfolio row that says "waiting its turn"**: normal. Three
  companies are researched at a time so none of them is rushed; the row
  starts by itself when a slot frees. You can close the tab.
- **A portfolio row that says "could not be finished"**: the workspace
  exists and works, but its research did not land. Open it and use
  *Rescan your site* at the foot of [Your brief](/settings/brief).
- **"Skipped …: already has a workspace"** on an upload: your agency is
  already on that company's workspace, so a second one was not created.
  Switch to it from the workspace switcher.
- **"The studio cannot send this run as it is configured"**: a fault at our
  end, caught before the run started, so nothing was spent and nothing was
  lost. Every run is checked against the shape the model will accept before
  the job is created; a run refused this way would have failed several
  minutes in. It is logged for us automatically. Try again in an hour, and
  tell us if it is still there.

# Cookies, and what is kept on your device

## The short answer

Prospektor stores ten small things on the device you are reading this on, and
every one of them is either signing you in, remembering a preference you
set about your own screen, or holding what you typed until you send it. There is
**no advertising, no fingerprinting and no third-party tracker that runs on its own**:
the studio's pages make no request to any other company by default, not even
for typefaces. The one third party that could see anything is **Microsoft
Clarity**, which records session replays and heatmaps of the studio so we can
see where it confuses people. The studio does not load it today: it exists
only where a deployment is set up with it, and ours is not yet. Once it is, it
loads only after you switch analytics on
in the cookie notice, and every word on the screen is masked before a replay
leaves your browser, so nothing you research, nobody's name and no draft you
are writing reaches Microsoft. Off, nothing about your visit reaches anybody
else.

Three things *are* counted, on Prospektor's own servers rather than on your
device, and they are set out in [What Prospektor counts about your
use](#what-prospektor-counts-about-your-use) below. Until 24 August 2026 this
page said "no analytics" without that paragraph, which was true of your
browser and not true of the product. It is corrected here and in the panel
itself, and the flat phrase "no analytics tool" is gone from both, because
one of those three records is exactly the thing an analytics company would be
hired to do. We do it ourselves, on our own servers, and say so.

That is why the notice you saw on your first visit had a **Got it** button
rather than an Accept and a Reject. There is nothing optional to accept or
reject yet, and a choice over nothing is worse than no question at all.
The notice and the panel behind it read in your workspace's language
(**Workspace settings → Workspace → Language**); the cookies' own names stay as your
browser shows them.

## Seeing the list yourself

**Cookies** in the footer of any page, or the address
`studio.prospektor.ai/#cookies`, opens the full list: what each item is
called, whether it is a cookie or browser storage, what it is for, and how
long it stays. The code works from the same list, so it cannot drift out of
date without a test failing.

| What | Kind | For | Kept |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pps_session` | Cookie | Keeps you signed in, remembers which workspace you picked, and notes when you last saved something so the next screen reads your save and not an older copy | 12 hours |
| `pps_oauth_state` | Cookie | Protects the Google sign-in round trip | 10 minutes |
| `pps_share` | Cookie | Remembers which shared pitch sent you to sign in, so you land back on it | 10 minutes |
| `pps-theme` | Local storage | This device's light/dark choice | Until you clear site data |
| `pps-consent` | Local storage | Your answer to the cookie notice, and when you gave it | 12 months |
| `pps-example-gone` | Local storage | That you removed the example pitch from your library | Until you clear site data |
| `pps-language` | Local storage | The language this device last read the studio in, so the next visit loads its words at once | Until you clear site data |
| `pps-steps-skipped` | Local storage | Which getting-started steps you skipped, so they stay off Home's setup card on this device | Until you clear site data |
| `pps-report` | Local storage | Which week's report this device has seen, and which of its blockers you marked not relevant, so neither comes back on this device | Until you clear site data |
| `pps-draft` | Session storage | What you typed into a box and have not sent yet, so a reload gives it back. This tab only, and gone the moment you send it | Until you send it or close the tab |
| Microsoft Clarity | Script + cookies | Heatmaps and session replay of the studio, every word masked, so we can see where it confuses people. Only where a deployment names a project, and only after you switch analytics on | 1 year |

Every `pps-` key but one is stored on the device and nowhere else.
The Appearance choice is the exception since #97: when you are signed in it
is also written to your account profile, with the moment you chose it, so
your other devices start the same way. Nobody but you reads it, your
colleagues are unaffected, and nothing in the product is decided by it.

## What Prospektor counts about your use

None of these is a cookie and none involves another company. They are records
kept on Prospektor's servers, and this page names them because a page titled
*what is kept about me* that stopped at cookies would be answering an easier
question than the one you asked. The same four are listed in the **Cookies**
panel in the studio's footer, in the same words the code works from.

### When you were last here

Per member, per workspace: your email address, when you first and last opened
the studio here, when you last signed in, how many separate days you have been
here, how many times you have signed in, and whether the last sign-in came
through Google or an emailed link.

**Not** what you looked at. No page, no screen, no search, no pitch, no scroll
and no dwell time; the record is written when you arrive and knows nothing
about what you did next.

It is written on the studio's own start-up call, at most once an hour. It
exists so a workspace nobody has opened in a month gets a conversation rather
than an invoice. Only Prospektor's operator sees it, on the monitoring screen;
not your colleagues, not the agency above you, and nowhere in the product. It
is deleted with the workspace.

### Nothing in the emails

The mail Prospektor sends you carries **no open-tracking pixel and no rewritten
links**. Whether you opened it, and what you clicked in it, is not recorded
anywhere (not by us and not by our mail provider) because the messages never
ask for it. As of 30 August 2026 they carry no images at all.

### Which screens get opened

Per **workspace**, per screen: how many times it was opened, on how many
separate days, and the first and last of those days. Twenty-nine screen names and
a number beside each; that is the whole record.

**Not who.** There is no address in it, no name and no session marker, so it
cannot say who opened anything, only that somebody in this workspace did.
**Not when, beyond the day**: no clock time is kept, so it cannot be
reassembled into a session even in principle. **Not in what order**: it is a
tally, not a trail. And never *which* pitch: a pitch you open is counted as
"a pitch", never as that one. Nothing about a company, a search, a target or
anything you typed goes anywhere near it.

It exists so that a screen nobody can find gets fixed instead of guessed at.
Before this, the only way to know which parts of the studio people actually
use was to ask them, and the honest way to ask (a consent banner for an
analytics vendor) would have been answered by a small minority and would have
sent your visit to another company. This sends it nowhere. Only Prospektor's
operator sees it, as counts on the monitoring screen.

**Your browser can switch this one off by itself.** If it sends a Global
Privacy Control signal (below), nothing is counted from it at all. That works
here and not for the two records around it, for an honest reason: these counts
are sent by the page you are reading, so a browser refusing to send them stops
the counting for real, while a switch over something written on our servers
would not stop anything. We would rather have a smaller number than a switch
that lies.

### How long an edit takes

When you fix a block of a deliverable and press **Save & teach**, the studio
records how long that block was open before you saved it: the moment you
pressed the pencil, the moment you pressed save, and the gap between them. Three
fields on the run: when, which kind of deliverable, and the number of
milliseconds.

**Not what you wrote, and not who wrote it.** The record carries no address of
its own, nothing you typed, no keystrokes, no screen and no navigation. One
duration per save, and nothing at all about the minutes between.

**Not a number where there is no honest one.** If the duration arrives unusable,
or if it is longer than thirty minutes (a tab somebody walked away from is not
half an hour of work) it is stored as *no clock* rather than rounded to
something plausible. It is never stored as zero, which would claim the draft
needed no fixing when what really happened is that nothing was measured.

It exists because of what this product is. Prospektor writes a first draft and
expects you to fix it, so the only honest measure of whether a draft was any
good is how long the fixing took, and it is the number that says whether a
change we made to the studio actually helped or only felt like it did. It is
read as a median across many runs; no single edit of yours decides anything.
Only Prospektor's operator sees it. Not your colleagues, not the agency above
you, not the person you shared a pitch with, and nowhere in the product.

**Your browser can switch this one off by itself too.** If it sends a Global
Privacy Control signal (below), the studio does not send the duration at all;
and your edit saves exactly as it would have. What a refusal drops is the
measurement, never the work.

### The life of this workspace

About the workspace rather than about you: when it was created, which door it
came through, its plan, and the dates it was suspended, resumed or ended. No
address, no company name, nothing anybody typed or produced.

Since 24 Aug it also holds **which option was picked** if the subscription was
paused or cancelled from inside the studio. That question is multiple choice and
has no text box anywhere, deliberately, so what is kept is one token from a
fixed list, never a sentence. If you would rather say more, the email that may
follow asks for a reply and you can ignore it.

This one deliberately outlives the workspace it describes; otherwise the
question *do customers stay?* could only ever be asked of the customers who
did. When a workspace is deleted the record is re-keyed to a one-way hash and
marked erased, so the arithmetic survives without you surviving in it.

### If you would rather we did not

All four run on **legitimate interest** rather than on consent, which is why
there is no switch for them in the Cookies panel; a switch that has to say yes
is worse than an honest sentence. What you have instead is the right to object,
under Article 21 of the GDPR. (For *Which screens get opened* and *How long an
edit takes*, a Global Privacy Control signal from your browser already is that
objection, and is honoured without you writing to anyone; those two are the
ones your own browser sends, so refusing genuinely stops them.)

Write to [privacy@prospektor.ai](mailto:privacy@prospektor.ai). A person answers
every one: either we stop counting you, or we tell you why we believe we may
continue, and if you disagree with that answer you can take it to your
supervisory authority. Nothing about your account changes while you wait, and
objecting is never a reason for anything in the studio to work differently.

## Changing your mind

Click **Cookies** in the footer. Whatever you chose, the same panel that set
it will unset it, from any page, with no sign-in and no email to anyone. If
you clear your browser's site data, the answer goes with it and you will be
asked again on your next visit.

You will also be asked again if twelve months pass, or if we ever change what
we store; an answer to one version of this notice is not treated as an
answer to a different one.

## If your browser says no on your behalf

Some browsers and extensions send a **Global Privacy Control** signal, which
is a standing "do not sell or share my information". Prospektor reads that as
a refusal of everything optional and records it that way without asking you
again. You can still turn something on from the Cookies panel if you want to.

It does one more thing, added 24 August 2026: it stops *Which screens get
opened* counting your visit at all, and since 25 August 2026 it also stops
*How long an edit takes* being measured, while your edit saves exactly as it
would have. Those two are the records your browser can switch off on its own,
because they are the two your browser is the one sending. The other two are
written on our servers, where a switch would stop nothing and saying otherwise
would be a lie in the shape of a feature.

## Why there is a panel at all if nothing is optional

Because of what comes next. The panel is the gate anything loaded into your
browser would have to come through, and it is switched on before there is
anything to gate rather than after. If Prospektor ever adds an analytics tool,
three things happen at once and none of them is optional for us: it appears in
that list with its name and its purpose, the notice turns into a real Accept
and Reject with equal weight, and it does not load at all until you have said
yes.

The three records above are the other kind of thing, and the panel now says so
in the same breath rather than leaving them to a policy page. A gate is the
right answer for something that would run in your browser; for something that
runs on our servers under legitimate interest, the right answer is to name it
and to make objecting easy.

## Your phone number, and your passkeys

Two things we hold about **you** rather than about your work, both added
24 August 2026:

- **A phone number**, if you gave one, in [Your account](/settings/account),
  or on a free run, where a mobile is asked for before we will email you the
  result. One number is held per person, and a number already on your account is
  never replaced by one typed on a free run. It is never sent to a model and never
  included in a pitch, a proposal or a shared link. One third party can receive it,
  and only on a free run with the box left ticked: Sendblue, the texting service
  our product news by text will be sent from, gets the number, your address and the
  domain you ran, as a contact, never as a message from us. Sendblue is not
  connected yet, so today the number goes nowhere else; this page changes
  before it is. Untick the box,
  clear the number, or withdraw the text permission below and that contact is
  deleted there too. What it may be **used** for is exactly what you have allowed: getting you
  back into your account and reaching you about the account itself, always; and
  product news by text only if that permission is granted, which is one of the
  four below and can be withdrawn at any time. On a free run that box starts
  ticked; unticking it means the number is not stored at all. Clear a stored
  number any time in [Your account](/settings/account).
- **Your passkeys**, if you made any, and specifically only their **public**
  halves. The private key never leaves your device and we never see it. We keep
  no information about the make or model of your device, no IP address and no
  browser fingerprint: a passkey record is a public key, a coarse label like
  "This device", when it was made and when it was last used.

- **Your contact permissions**: which of product email, account texts, product
  texts and phone calls you have allowed, when you last changed each one, and
  whether you answered on the first card or in settings. Withdrawals are
  recorded the same way grants are, so there is always an answer to "what did I
  agree to, and when". **Nothing is actually sent through any of these
  channels**: Prospektor has no mailing list, no connected text-message
  provider (Sendblue, above, once connected, will hold contacts and send
  nothing on its own) and nobody making calls. If that ever changes, this page changes first.

The first two belong to your account rather than to a workspace, so deleting a
workspace does not remove them. Removing a passkey in *Your account* does; so does asking
us to erase your account data at
[privacy@prospektor.ai](mailto:privacy@prospektor.ai).

## Share links

If someone sent you a Prospektor link and you are reading their work rather
than using the studio, the same is true of that page: strictly necessary
cookies only, no third-party requests, and the same **Cookies** link in its
footer. The person who shared it can see that the link was opened; what they
see, and what the sender's workspace knows about you, is set out in the
[privacy policy](https://prospektor.ai/privacy/#viewers).

# Connect your Claude

Your own Claude can do the work in this workspace: read a company, write the
pitch, prep the call, map who you know, say what to do next, record what
happened.

## Do you need a token?

| What you are connecting | How | Token? |
|---|---|---|
| claude.ai | Add a custom connector | **No** |
| ChatGPT | Add a custom connector | **No** |
| Claude Code | `claude mcp add` | Yes |
| Claude Desktop | `mcp-remote` in the config file | Yes |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | Yes |

claude.ai and ChatGPT connect by their own connector screen. They mint the
token themselves and put it on your Claude tile; there is nothing to copy and
nothing to paste. Start at *From claude.ai or ChatGPT* below.

Everything else pastes a token:

1. **Workspace settings → Connect your apps → Your own agent → New token.**
   Label it "Claude", tick what it may do, press **Mint**.
2. Press **Copy setup for your agent**.
3. Paste it into Claude Code, Cursor or Claude Desktop. It asks which tool you
   use and wires it up.

The paste carries the server address, your token and the config for each
client, so the agent does the rest.

## What it can do

| Tool | What it does | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| `scan_company` | Reads a company from its website. A reading that failed says why, and is asked again an hour on. | A scan from the token's daily budget. |
| `build_pitch` | Researches a company and writes the pitch in your voice, deliverables included. Several minutes. | A run. |
| `prep_for_call` | A one-page sheet for a call at a named stage. About a minute. | A run. |
| `who_do_we_know` | Who you already know at a company, at once: the imported people who work there, with their role and which import they came from, and the brief's own lines that mention it. | Nothing. |
| `find_warm_paths` | Who in your imported network could open the door at a company, researched: each path with its evidence, the ask and the note the connector sends on. Name the company, or a finished pitch. About a minute. | A run. |
| `list_doors` | Who you already know: every company on your shelf or in your library that somebody in the network reaches, best door first. | Nothing. |
| `record_intro` | Where an introduction stands: asked, they said yes, no, or meeting booked. | Nothing, ever. |
| `push_to_crm` | Sends a finished pitch to the CRM your workspace has connected: the company, its people, a deal and a note that cites the sources. Pushing it again updates. With `dryRun: true` it writes nothing and answers every write the push would make, with the exact payload, so Claude can show you what lands before it lands. | A run. |
| `next_step` | Paste their reply or your meeting notes. Back comes where the deal stands, the one next step, the message it needs in your voice, and a checklist. About a minute. | A run. |
| `tick_step` | Ticks a line on that checklist. | Nothing, ever. |
| `get_pitch` | One saved pitch, by id or by company. Says of each deliverable whether it was written, failed (and why) or was never asked for. | Nothing. |
| `list_library` | The index of what is saved: company, score, verdict. Never the pitch itself. | Nothing. |
| `job_status` | Where a running job has got to. Done means the whole result, sources included, and, per deliverable, written, failed with the reason, pending or not requested. | Nothing. |
| `record_outcome` | What happened with a company. Every outcome sharpens the next pitch. | Nothing, ever. |
| `whoami` | What the token holds and how much day is left. | Nothing, ever. |

Long jobs answer with a job id. Your assistant polls `job_status` until the
status is `done`. A pitch takes several minutes, so it will wait between polls.

`next_step` reads what is on the company's outcome record (the same notes
you see under **Outcomes**) with what you just pasted on top. Ask it again
with only the company a minute later and it answers with the step. Paste what
changed to plan afresh; the newest material decides.

`push_to_crm` needs a CRM connected first; the workspace's owner does that
once under **Workspace settings → Connect your apps**. With none connected the
tool says so rather than guessing one.

Every answer carries its sources. A pitch says which pages it read, who it
decided the company is, and what compliance found. Nothing is held back that
the studio itself would show you.

## Which scopes to tick

The paste works with whatever the token holds. For the whole set:

| Tick | To get |
|---|---|
| `scan:run` | `scan_company` |
| `work:run` | `build_pitch`, `prep_for_call`, `find_warm_paths`, `push_to_crm`, `next_step`, `job_status` |
| `library:read` | `get_pitch`, `list_library`, `who_do_we_know`, `list_doors` |
| `context:write` | `record_outcome`, `tick_step`, `record_intro` |

A token for a colleague's Claude that should read but never spend gets
`library:read` alone.

## Wiring it by hand

The server is `https://studio.prospektor.ai/api/mcp`, streamable HTTP. Send
the token as a bearer header.

Claude Code:

```
claude mcp add --transport http prospektor https://studio.prospektor.ai/api/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer psk_…"
```

Cursor, in `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```
{"mcpServers":{"prospektor":{"url":"https://studio.prospektor.ai/api/mcp","headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer psk_…"}}}}
```

A client that cannot send a header, Claude Desktop among them, goes through
`mcp-remote`:

```
{"mcpServers":{"prospektor":{"command":"npx","args":["-y","mcp-remote","https://studio.prospektor.ai/api/mcp","--header","Authorization: Bearer psk_…"]}}}
```

## From claude.ai or ChatGPT

Their connector screens have no box for a token, and need none.

**claude.ai:**

1. **Settings**, then **Connectors** in the left sidebar, under *Customize*.
   On a Team or Enterprise plan an owner adds it once under *Organization
   settings → Connectors*, and everyone else presses **Connect** afterwards.
2. Press **Add** at the top right of the Connectors panel and pick the
   custom-connector option. Prospektor is not in the directory below; that
   button is the way in.
3. Paste `https://studio.prospektor.ai/api/mcp` and press **Add**. Leave
   *Advanced settings* alone; there is no client id or secret to fill in.
4. Prospektor opens. Signed out, it asks you to sign in and comes back here.
5. Press **Connect**.
6. In a chat, press **+**, then **Connectors**, and switch Prospektor on.

**ChatGPT:** *Settings → Apps → Advanced settings*, switch on **Developer
mode**, then **Add custom connector** and the same address. On Plus and Pro,
ChatGPT's custom connectors are read-only: it will scan and read your library
and refuse to spend a run. Business, Enterprise and Edu get the whole set.

### The screen it opens

One screen, one button. It is headed **Connect Claude**, says *It will work in
**your workspace** as you, and the connection goes to **claude.ai***, and shows
five boxes with four ticked: read a company, start work that spends a run, read
a saved pitch, record an outcome. *Take a copy of this workspace out* is always
left unticked; tick it only if you want the app to be able to export. Then
**Connect**, or *Not now*.

An app names itself, so check the address after *goes to*. If the heading says
Claude and the address is not claude.ai, press *Not now*.

Only the workspace's owner can connect an app; a member gets one sentence
naming the owner to ask. A paused workspace says so and connects nothing.

### Check it worked

Ask your assistant *what is this workspace wired to*. It answers with your
workspace's name, the token's label and how much of the day is left; the
name is the proof it is pointed at the right workspace.

The connection is a token row under **Workspace settings → Connect your apps →
Claude**, labelled with the app's name; the row says when it was last used and how many calls it
has made. **Revoke** stops the app at once. It renews itself every thirty days
for as long as it is used.

## The same verbs over plain HTTP

Every tool is also a route on `/api/v1`, for a script or a CRM:

| Route | Tool |
|---|---|
| `POST /api/v1/pitch` · `GET /api/v1/pitch?id=…` | `build_pitch` · `job_status` |
| `POST /api/v1/prep` · `GET /api/v1/prep?id=…` | `prep_for_call` · `job_status` |
| `POST /api/v1/paths` · `GET /api/v1/paths?id=…` · `PATCH /api/v1/paths` | `find_warm_paths` · `job_status` · `record_intro` |
| `GET /api/v1/network?company=…` | `who_do_we_know` |
| `GET /api/v1/doors` | `list_doors` |
| `POST /api/v1/crm` | `push_to_crm` |
| `POST /api/v1/next` · `GET /api/v1/next?company=…` · `PATCH /api/v1/next` | `next_step` · `tick_step` |
| `GET /api/v1/library?id=…` or `?company=…` | `get_pitch` |
| `GET /api/v1/library[?q=…]` | `list_library` |

Scans, outcomes, `whoami` and exports are on the same surface. See *API
tokens* under the workspace help for the day cap and how to revoke.

## What it costs

A run from your Claude is a run. A free workspace has its one full pitch, and
your assistant meets the same wall you would. Runs past that need a
subscription. The token's day cap is 1,000 calls; `whoami`, `record_outcome`,
`tick_step` and `record_intro` never count.

## When something goes wrong

- **"This token does not hold work:run"**: mint one that does. Tokens never
  gain a scope after minting.
- **"Free workspaces run one full pitch, and this one has run it"**: the
  free run is spent. Subscribe to run the rest.
- **"Nothing to map yet"**: import who you know first, under *Your network*.
- **"Nothing on record for …"**: `next_step` plans from the company's outcome
  record. Paste what they said in `note`, or record an outcome first.
- **Still queued after ten minutes**: a run hit its limit. Start it again.
- **401 with a date**: the token expired. Mint another.
- **The connector adds but no Prospektor screen appears**: the address is
  wrong. It is `/api/mcp`, not `/mcp` or `/api/v1`.
- **"Only the workspace's owner can connect an app"**: you are signed in as a
  member; the screen names who to ask.
- **"This page had expired. Connect the app again."**: the consent screen sat
  open too long. Add the connector again.
- **ChatGPT lists the tools and refuses to run a pitch**: the Plus and Pro
  read-only limit above, not a fault.

Revoke a token from **Workspace settings → Connect your apps → Revoke**.
Everything holding
it stops at once.

# The first visit, in detail

[Getting started](/help/getting-started) is the short path: three sessions,
a task at each step. This page is the long version of the same first visit,
kept for when a step raises a question the short one does not answer: the
free run before you have an account, the free workspace, what the studio does
in your first minutes, and the account chores that wait until later.

Prospektor is a workspace where a sales team researches target
companies and drafts partner pitches. You type a company; the studio works
out who that company actually is from its own website, researches it, scores
partnership fit against what your workspace says it is hunting for, and
drafts your enabled deliverables: pitch deck, one-pager, cold-email
sequence, written proposal, plus a decision-maker list and lookalike
companies to pitch next.

## Before you have an account: the free run

You do not need a workspace, a card or even an email address to see what
Prospektor finds. A **free run** lives at `/r` on the studio: type any company
website (or just their name) and the studio does the first half of its job in
front of you.

1. **It reads the site**: what that company sells and to whom, and two or
   three things visibly true from their own pages. Where we can confirm them,
   the first facts on the strip are checked against a company database rather
   than read off the page: headcount, location, industry. It says so underneath, and
   it counts: *"Read just now: 1 page and 2 web searches of acme.com."* If it
   ever says *"nothing here was opened just now"* instead, that is the studio
   telling you the truth rather than dressing a guess up as a reading. Check
   what it says about you and correct the next step if it is off.
2. **It says what it thinks you should be hunting for**: one sentence naming
   the kind of company worth approaching. This is a guess, and it is meant to
   be corrected: *"That's not it. Let me say"* opens a box, and one line in
   your own words ("agencies that resell hosting", "family offices in the
   Nordics") sends it looking for those instead.
3. **It finds real companies**: three of them, each with its own website, two
   or three checkable facts, a fit score on the same 0–100 scale a paid run
   uses, and one sentence on why this company.

Then, if you want it, one more thing: **who you are up against**. *Name a
competitor* takes one rival's website and reads them the way it read you: what
they sell, how they position themselves, our read of what they actually do, who
they sell to, and **a list of their clients with the page that names each one**.
Their clients are your prospect list, which is why that list is the point of the
block rather than a footnote. One rival per free run.

One line of that report is deliberately blank. *How you win* is the only line a
competitor's own website could never answer, because it comes from your brief,
so the free version says it needs one instead of guessing at a slogan. A
workspace writes it.

Then it stops. What a free run gives you is **who to approach**. What a
workspace gives you is **what to send them**: the pitch in your own voice, the
deliverables, the decision-makers, the prep sheet, and a source behind every
claim. That is the line, and the free run says so on the page rather than
springing it on you.

Every free run has its own address, `/r/<token>`, and it keeps working. Send
it to a colleague and they see the whole thing. They are not asked to sign in,
because there is nothing to sign in to. Nothing about a free run is listed,
indexed or searchable: the link is the only way to it, so it is as private as
whoever you send it to.

**If you would rather not lose it, we will send it to you.** *While you wait*
appears under the steps as the run works, and again at the bottom of a finished
run: an email address and a mobile number, both needed to have the run sent.
The run does not wait for either: the companies appear whether you fill this
in or not, and the link in your address bar works either way.

Under those fields there is one box, *Product news and tips, by email and text*,
and it starts **ticked**. Untick it and nothing at all is kept: no list, no
record, and the number you typed is not stored. You get the link and that is
the end of it. Leave it ticked and you get the same news a customer gets, a few
times a month at most, by email and sometimes by text, and every one of those
emails carries a one-click unsubscribe that works without signing in to
anything. It is the same permission the studio asks for on your first day with
an account, so if you later buy a workspace you will not be asked twice, and you
can change it any time in [Your account](/settings/account) → *How we may reach
you*.

Your number is held the way an account's is: in full international form, one per
person, and a number you have already set on an account is never replaced by one
typed here. Deleting your data deletes it with everything else; see
[Privacy](/help/privacy).

### "Why did I get an email about a run I did weeks ago?"

If you ran a free run, left that box ticked and never opened a workspace, you
may get **one** email pointing you back at your own run. One, ever, not a
sequence, and there is no second one waiting behind it. It links to your
`/r/<token>` and to nothing else, so it opens without signing in, the same way
it did the day you ran it.

The unsubscribe link on it stops that email **and** the product news it was sent
on: they are the same permission, so one click ends both. If you have already
opened a workspace you are not on the list at all, and if you unticked the box
there is no record of you to be on it.

A free run is genuinely free and it is capped for the day as a whole, so
occasionally it will ask you to come back tomorrow. A company somebody has
already run comes back instantly and costs nothing, and the same is true of
competitor reports, which have a smaller daily cap of their own because they are
a much bigger piece of work.

## The free workspace: one full pitch

Signing up gets you a workspace of your own, and everything a paid one does
right up to the second run.

If you came from a free run and corrected what it said you were hunting for,
that sentence comes with you: the studio opens your brief on your words instead
of asking you the question again. Correct it there any time; **Your brief**
shows whose sentence it is.

You answer the onboarding, the studio reads your site and writes your brief,
and **Leads for you** fills with real companies it thinks you should approach. The
first question is who your dream customer would be, and the second is what you are
hunting for; the research is written to answer both: your sentences reach the read of your site,
so the fit thesis and the motion list come back for the companies you actually
want rather than for whatever your homepage suggests. Press **Glance** on
one, then **Prospekt**, and you get the whole thing: the research, the fit case,
who decides, and every deliverable your workspace has switched on, written in
your voice, with a source behind each claim.

That is the one run. After it, `/upgrade` is what you meet when you press the
next one. You can also open it by address at any time, and **Settings → Plan**
has the same door.

**Nothing is taken away.** Your brief, your pitch, your library and the rest of
the leads on **Leads for you** stay exactly where they are, readable and shareable.
What stops is starting the next run: a second pitch, a glance, a competitor
report, a call prep sheet, an inbound judgment, warm paths, a rescan, a whole
list at once through Beast Mode. A subscription starts them again immediately,
on the same workspace, with the work already in it.

The competitor report that stops is the one written **from your brief**: your
read, your suppress list, a Prospekt button on each of their clients, and *How
you win* filled in. **That button then keeps score**: press it and the card
says **Running** with a way to watch, and once the pitch lands it says **Open
the pitch**. Both are worked out fresh every time the report is opened, so a
report you ran weeks ago is still the shortest way back to every pitch it
started. A company already on your suppress list never gets the button at all. The neutral version at a free run is still free to anyone,
and still leaves that line blank.

The studio still talks to you about that one pitch: **Ask the studio** under its *Why them*,
**Make sense of this** on its outcome, the support chat and the home box all
work. They share a daily allowance, smaller on a free workspace than on a paid
one, and when it is spent for the day the studio says so and answers again
tomorrow. It is not the upgrade screen.

Two things worth knowing. The **one run belongs to the workspace, not to you**,
so a free account holds one workspace, and being invited into a colleague's
changes nothing. And **asking what a run would cost is always free**, whether
or not you have spent yours.

## Your first minutes

- **Sign-in** is Google, a passkey, or an emailed link; there are no
  passwords. Access is your workspace's email allowlist; if your address is
  on it, you are in. Adding a **passkey** takes one press in
  [Your account](/settings/account), and after that signing in
  is Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello or a security key, with nothing to type
  and no link to wait for. See *Signing in* below.
- **Value first, account chores last.** The first time you sign in, the
  studio leads with the work: you land on Home, which says what the studio is
  doing while it sets up and asks who already buys from you. Your first three
  companies appear there, in the spot the empty cards held, as soon as they
  are found, with a short setup card under them. What the account still needs: a
  **recovery phone number** (so we can get you back in if you lose access to
  your email), **how we may reach you** (all optional, all off unless you
  tick them), and, if nobody here has confirmed it yet, **what your company
  is called**. It waits as one quiet *Complete your account info* line on the
  dashboard, and can always be answered later in
  [Your account](/settings/account).
- **One question comes before your company name: whose studio this is**, either
  *My own company*, or *A client of mine*. An agency picking the second gets
  the six questions below asked about their client rather than about them,
  deliverables written as the client and never mentioning the agency, and a
  workspace name somebody is still asked to confirm. Leave both alone and it
  reads as your own, which is what it always did. Change it any time in
  [Workspace settings](/settings/workspace) → *Whose studio this is*.
- A brand-new workspace opens with a **first draft**, not with a question. The
  studio reads your own website and leads with the two things that are work
  rather than facts about you: who it would go and find, and the paragraph it
  would open with in your voice. **What else we read** opens the rest: what it
  read off your site, where it would look, who you are up against, and what it
  would score those companies against. Every block says where its text came
  from (our guess from your site, or your own words) and a block only you can
  fill stays empty rather than being filled in with something plausible. Where
  somebody has already scanned your domain, the draft starts from confirmed
  company data (industry, headcount, founding year) instead of guessing at it.
  Where you *sell* is never guessed from where you are registered: it stays
  empty until you say.
- **A workspace an agency made for you opens the way the agency chose.** Their
  create form ends on two doors. **Invite them to set it up** means the
  questions below are yours: they wait for you the first time you sign in, and
  the invite says so. **Set it up yourself** means the agency answered them for
  you, about you, before the research was trusted; you land in the studio
  itself, on the suggested leads. Either of you can finish or change the answers
  any time from [Your brief](/settings/brief).
- **Then one question: what first?** The draft is followed by a fork: three
  doors, with *Leads for you* already chosen, and **Continue** the only
  button, so the usual act is a single press. The other two doors are
  *a competitor's clients* (name one rival, get the list of who they sell to)
  and *lookalikes of your customers* (name two, get companies like them). Take
  either of those and you are in front of that question straight away instead
  of behind six others. Nothing is lost, because the door you skipped is
  still there afterwards: your three suggested companies still arrive,
  [Counterprospekt](/competitors) still takes a competitor's name, and
  **Lookalikes** stands on the home screen for good. The six questions move
  behind the door, onto [Your brief](/settings/brief).
- Underneath it is a short **interview**, six questions: **who your dream
  customer would be**, what to hunt for, **where and how big**, **a few
  competitors by name**, **a few customers and why they are good ones**, how
  you want to sound. Each screen is one calm question and the field that
  answers it, nothing else, and each answer sharpens that draft and every
  future pitch: your sentence replaces our guess in the brief. They are asked
  while the studio researches your company in the background, every one of
  them is answerable from the first second, and you can skip all six and come
  back via [Your brief](/settings/brief). **Take me in** works from every
  screen, and your workspace already exists behind it.

### The example pitch in your library

Your [Library](/library) is not empty on day one. There is one pitch in it
already, labelled **Example**, and it is there so you can read a finished run
while your own are still going; your three take a few minutes each, and the
example takes none.

- **It is invented, and identical in every workspace.** Harborline Freight and
  Ledgerpost are both made up. Nothing in it was researched, and its 94 is the
  example's own score, not a judgment the studio made about anything of yours.
- **It shows the real screen.** The fit thesis, the deck, the sequence
  sequence, the one-pager, the proposal, the decision-makers and the lookalikes
  are laid out exactly where your own runs put them.
- **It is read-only.** No pencil, no share link, no call prep, and its
  lookalikes cannot be run. It is an illustration, so it never touches your
  brief, your voice or your outcomes.
- **Remove** takes it away in one press and it stays away on this device, and
  it goes on its own as soon as your first real pitch lands.

### Who would be your dream customer?

The first question, and the one most worth answering. A website is often years
behind the customer a company actually wants, and a brief drafted from the
website scores your dream client against yesterday's shape. Your own words fix
that in one line.

- **One per line: the company, then why that one.** *"Fashion Nova, they shoot
  weekly drops at volume"* is a complete answer. Two is plenty.
- **It reaches the score, not only the leads.** The answer goes onto [Ideal
  customer](/settings/hunt), the first box on that page, and as a line in your own words, and every glance and every
  full pitch reads those lines above what the studio drafted from your site. A
  company that matches one of them is what you asked for, and a drafted line
  that would rule it out for its size or shape yields to it.
- **It is not the customers question.** A company named as a customer joins
  *Do not contact* and is never approached. A dream client is the opposite: the
  one you most want approached. Keep the two apart.
- **Change it any time.** The same box is the first thing on Ideal customer;
  edit it there and Save, and the lines it wrote move with it.

### Name a few customers, and why they are good ones

The fifth question is the highest-value thirty seconds in the interview after
the dream client, and the **why** is the reason.

- **Two or three is plenty; five is better.** One per line: the company, then
  what makes that one good. *"Northwind — their CFO had the same problem"* is a
  complete answer.
- **Customers you already have.** The ones you wish you had are the dream
  client question above, because a company named here is never approached.
- **The names alone are not the point.** Anyone can find companies that look
  like a list of names. What the studio cannot guess is *why* those are the good
  ones, and that reason becomes the thesis every prospect is scored against.
- **What you want more of** sits beside it, with two one-tap suggestions.
  *More companies like these* keeps the studio close to what already works;
  *Adjacent markets, related to these* treats your customers as a starting point
  and looks for the neighbouring category your strengths carry into. It is a box
  rather than a switch, so *"mostly more like these, but I want to test
  facilities management"* is a real answer.
- **A long list goes in as a file.** *Upload a list* beside the box takes a CSV
  or a paste, the company in the first column and its website in the second.
  The file is read in your browser and never uploaded anywhere.
- **The two lists do different jobs.** The few in the box carry the reasons, and
  those are what every prospect is scored against. An uploaded list is simply
  who you already sell to: every company on it joins *Do not contact*, so no run is
  ever spent pitching one of them, and the suggestion search reads the list for
  the pattern those companies share.
- **The names in the box seed your first three companies.** The search that
  fills [Leads for you](/leads) hunts from them, and what you typed beside them
  decides how: closest honest matches, or the neighbouring category. None of
  the companies you named comes back as its own suggestion. Name nobody and the
  search works from your brief instead.

Both are on [Ideal customer](/settings/hunt) afterwards, and editable there, where
the same *Upload a list* takes a longer list later.

### Where should we hunt, and how big?

The third question is two plain boxes with one-tap suggestions under each, and
it is worth thirty seconds because everything the studio does afterwards reads
it: which companies are suggested to you, which ones a run goes looking for,
and how each is scored.

- **Geography** arrives pre-filled with our guess from your own site. Write
  over it in whatever words you like: `Germany`, `English-speaking countries`,
  `DACH`, `the Nordics plus the Netherlands`, or `Anywhere`. There is no list
  to pick from, on purpose; most real answers are not a country.
- **Company size** starts empty, because nothing on your website says what size
  of company *you* want to approach. `Mid-market and enterprise`, `startups
  under 50`, `exclude solopreneurs` are all fine answers, as is leaving it
  blank.
- Taps add up: a second suggestion joins the first (`Mid-market (51–500),
  Enterprise (500+)`), and tapping a lit one removes it.
- Both are **preferences, not filters.** A strong company just outside your
  stated area is still shown to you, and the pitch says plainly that it sits
  outside it, so the call stays yours. If you mean something absolute, say so
  in the box (`only Germany`, `never outside the EU`) and it is read that way.
- Answering the geography also makes web searches run from your own country
  where you named exactly one, so results come back the way they would for
  somebody sitting there rather than from a default locale.
- Change either at any time on [Ideal customer](/settings/hunt), and the next run
  uses the new answer.

### Name a few competitors

The third question asks who you are up against. Two or three names are
plenty, in whatever words you like, and it is skippable like everything else.
The studio never guesses your rivals off your site, so anything in this answer
is yours. It reads the names as a **map of your market**: suggestions hunt the
territory around them (companies that partner with those names, sell alongside
them, or serve the same buyers) and are told plainly that a company you
compete with is not one to suggest to you. The names also arrive on
[Counterprospekt](/competitors) as chips, where one tap runs that competitor's
report. Answer in whatever words you like: *"acme.com as well as
fieldlens.io"* becomes two chips, not one. Change or add names any time on
[Ideal customer](/settings/hunt); the deeper question on [Your brief](/settings/brief)
(*who do you lose to, and why do you win*) is separate, and sharpens how pitches answer the
objection rather than whom the studio targets.
- The **guided tour** opens when you press *Take the one-minute tour*, the
  last line of the setup card on Home, and walks eight steps, one per section of the sidebar, with its card and a ring
  travelling to the thing each step is about and one line on what that section
  is good for. Home, at the box you type in; [Leads for you](/leads), at the
  box you describe leads in; Research, on the example pitch with the ring round
  its tabs, which are what a finished pitch holds; [Counterprospekt](/competitors);
  Warm intros, at the paste box on [Your network](/network); Inbound, on
  [Prepare a call](/prep) with the form filled in for the example;
  [Library](/library); and [Settings](/settings/workspace), whose card says where
  *Support* is.
  It never opens on its own. Press *Take the one-minute tour* on Home or under
  Learn in Settings any time, and skipping it never loses anything.
- The home screen, [Leads](/), proposes companies worth pitching next,
  one card at a time; a thumbs-up starts a real pitch immediately. Each card's
  facts are read off that company's own website, which the studio opens while it
  is looking, rather than off a search result about them, so they are checkable
  by anyone who opens the same page. A card with only two facts on it is the
  studio declining to pad; a company it could not stand up at all is left off.
  A card leaves the shelf when you remove it, glance it or run it, including
  when you run that company from [Research prospekts](/pitch/new) instead, so the shelf
  never offers work you have already done. To remove one, press the **×** on
  the card and say which kind it is: **Not a fit**, or **Our client**. A card
  naming a company you already sell to is good news (the studio found your
  customers), and *Our client* puts it on [Do not contact](/suppress) as a
  customer and into your customers on [Ideal customer](/settings/hunt),
  and the next search hunts for more like it. Anything you glanced is in
  [Library](/library), where you can reopen it. The search for the next few starts the moment
  your first cards are handed to you, not once you have spent them, so there
  is normally something waiting by the time you come back. While the shelf is
  empty it says what of yours is running and links you to it.
- **A weak fit is never suggested.** The score on a card is out of 100:
  75 and up is a strong fit, 50 and up promising, and anything the search
  would score under 50 is held back rather than shown. You will see two cards,
  or one, or none, before you see a 42: a shelf that pads itself with a
  company nobody should call is a shelf you stop reading. When that leaves
  nothing to show, the screen says how many were held back and asks for the
  two answers that sharpen the next search most: **who already buys from
  you** and **who you compete with**, both on
  [Ideal customer](/settings/hunt).
- **The shelf learns from what you press.** A company you glance at and then
  research in full is the clearest thing you can tell the studio about what you
  want, clearer than your brief, because you looked and then you spent. From
  the second one of those, the next search hunts for that shape. It fades:
  a press stops counting after three months, so a curious click in week one
  does not steer you for ever. And one card a search is a deliberate bet
  *outside* that shape, marked **Adjacent bet** on the tile, because a shelf that only
  ever returns what you already pressed on narrows onto one kind of company and
  stops being worth opening. Where you have said which way to hunt on
  [Ideal customer](/settings/hunt), or typed what you are after, that decides
  instead and the studio does not second-guess it.
- **One question: who do you lose deals to?** It is the second door the
  interview offers, reached in one press if you take it. Name one and
  the studio reads their site and lists their clients. That list is your
  prospect list, and it lands in
  [Counterprospekt](/competitors). The box arrives carrying a competitor your
  brief already names, so the usual act is one press rather than one more
  question, and the name you give is written into your brief exactly as the
  interview's third question would have written it. *Skip* goes straight to
  the studio and nothing is lost; [Counterprospekt](/competitors) takes a
  competitor's name any time.
- **Lookalikes** is the other half of that idea: name customers you already
  have and the studio finds more companies like them. Its card is on Getting
  started; the box arrives carrying the customers you named at onboarding, so
  the usual act is one press. What comes back lands on [Leads for you](/leads) as ordinary cards: glance one for
  fifteen seconds to see the roles worth approaching, then press Prospekt.
  Adding *"— why they are a good one"* after a name tells the search which way
  to be alike; a name it has not heard before is written into your brief, and
  the reasons you gave at onboarding are never overwritten.
- **Home** (`/start`) is where signing in lands you, and it is the first
  entry in the sidebar.

  It opens with your name and one box whose placeholder shows what to type.
  Type what you want to do in your own words. Name a company and it takes you
  to the screen that researches it with the name already filled in; ask who
  decides at one, or for companies like your best customers, or for a rival's
  client list, and it opens that screen instead. *Prep my call with Nordic
  Threads* opens [Prepare a call](/prep) with the company filled in, and with the
  stage chosen when you said which call it is. *Companies like Fashion Nova* is
  a search for companies like that one. Lookalikes, which saves the names as
  your customers, opens only when you say they already are: *more like our
  customer Fashion Nova*. Nothing runs and nothing is
  charged: you land on the screen and press the button there. A question about
  the product, or a sentence it cannot place, opens the support chat with what
  you typed as the first message.

  Under the box, what is waiting, as pills you can press: runs still going,
  runs that stopped, pitches whose outcome nobody has recorded. Each one opens
  the screen that deals with it. Three at most, and nothing at all when nothing
  is waiting.

  Under the box, four chips for the asks people type most (*Give me leads*,
  *Who buys from a competitor*, *Who can introduce me*, *Prep a meeting*), one
  press each. Under those, the three leads worth a look: the top three cards
  of Leads for you, with **Glance** on each. Before the studio has looked, one
  button, **Get leads**. The greeting is *Welcome* on a first visit and
  *Welcome back* once your brief has its answers.

  The screen asks you nothing. What the studio still wants to know about your
  company is on [Your brief](/settings/brief), which says how many questions
  are left and takes the answers.

  Under Learn in Settings, **Prospektor Academy**: four short courses on your
  own leads, a list of asks to try in the bar, and *Take the one-minute tour*,
  so all three are always somewhere to go back to.
- Stuck at any point? **Support**, the round button at the bottom right of
  every screen, opens a chat
  that answers in seconds and remembers where you left off; its
  **💡 Request a feature** toggle sends an idea, an improvement or a bug
  report straight to the Prospektor team.

## The core loop

1. Open [Research prospekts](/pitch/new), enter a company name or domain (the field
   autocompletes and warns if your team already pitched them). Every box in the
   studio that takes a company name does the same (the [outcome
   editor](/outcomes), [Counterprospekt](/counter), the [suppress
   list](/suppress), a new client workspace) and picking a suggestion fills
   the website box beside it.
2. The run takes minutes and shows six live stages: understand, research,
   score, draft, people, check. You can leave any time: runs continue in the
   background and are listed under [Running](/running).
3. The finished pitch lands in the [Library](/library): summary, fit thesis,
   signals for and against, deliverables, decision-makers, lookalikes.
4. Edit any deliverable in place (the pencil). Saved edits teach the studio
   your team's voice (tone only, never facts) so future pitches sound more
   like you.
5. Record what happened on the card itself: press the badge, pick what
   happened. Closed deals feed the Leads shelf, so what it offers drifts
   toward what actually closes, and under those, the glances you paid to
   research in full.

## Pointing an AI assistant at Prospektor

[studio.prospektor.ai/llms.txt](https://studio.prospektor.ai/llms.txt) is the
door an agent reads: what Prospektor is, and the handful of calls it can make
without an account: a first look at any domain, what that look would cost, and
this whole documentation corpus as JSON.

There are no API keys yet, so an assistant cannot open your workspace, read your
briefs or start a pitch on your behalf. Everything in a workspace still needs a
person signed in.

## Signing in

There are three ways in, and they all check the same access list.

**A passkey** is the fastest and the safest. Add one from
[Your account](/settings/account) → *Add a passkey* while you are
signed in; your device makes a key, keeps the secret half where it can never
leave, and hands us only the public half. After that, going to the studio and
touching your fingerprint sensor is the whole sign-in. Most browsers offer the
passkey in the email field's own drop-down before you press anything, and
there is a **Sign in with a passkey** button underneath *Continue with Google*
for the ones that do not.

A passkey only works on this site, and that is the point: a convincing copy of
our sign-in page cannot ask your device for it, so there is nothing for anyone
to phish out of you.

You can add one on each device you use, see them all in *Your account*, and
remove any of them there. Removing a passkey stops it opening the studio; the
key your device still holds simply opens nothing.

**Google** is the front door for anyone with a Google account, and it is the
only door besides a passkey that can carry Prospektor's own operator role.

**An emailed link** is the fallback for an address that cannot use Google. It
works once and expires after 15 minutes, and your access is checked when you
use it rather than when it was sent. It opens a page naming the address it
signs in as; press **Continue** only if that is you and you asked for it.

## Your recovery phone number

We ask for it once, behind the *Complete your account info* line on the
dashboard, after your first leads and the tour, never in front of them, and
you can skip it. It is there so
that if you lose access to your email (the thing every other way in depends on)
there is still a way to get you back into an account you are paying for, and
so there is a way to reach you about the account itself.

Pick your country from the dropdown first, then write the number the way you
normally would: `0176 1234567` under Germany, `415 555 0134` under the United
States. Both become the same international number underneath. If you would
rather type the whole thing with a `+` in front, that works too and overrides
the dropdown.

It is used for nothing else unless you say so on the next question. It is never
sent to a model, never appears in a pitch, a proposal or a shared link, and is
never used for marketing without your say-so. Change it or clear it any time in
[Your account](/settings/account).

## How we may reach you

The same card asks which ways of contacting you are all right. Four separate
questions, **all off unless you turn them on**:

- **Product news and tips, by email**: what shipped and what other teams get
  out of it, a few times a month at most.
- **Text me about my account**: security alerts, and help getting back in.
- **Product news, by text**: the same news as the email, if a text suits you
  better.
- **You may call me**: about your account, or to ask what would make
  Prospektor more useful to you.

They are four questions rather than one on purpose: wanting a security text is
not the same as wanting a marketing one, and you should not have to take both
to get either.

If you bought your workspace on prospektor.ai, the payment step there carries
the same unticked *Product news and tips, by email* box. A tick given at
checkout is recorded against your address before you first sign in, so you are
not asked twice, and it is undone the same way as any other answer, in
[Your account](/settings/account) → *How we may reach you* or by
the one-click unsubscribe on any such email.

**Account email is not on that list, because it is not optional.** Sign-in
links, receipts and service notices come with having an account; there is no
way to turn those off and still have one.

Today none of these actually send anything: Prospektor has no mailing list, no
text-message provider and nobody making calls. We ask now because you are
already filling in a form, and turning any of them on or off later is one click
in [Your account](/settings/account).

## The getting-started course: eight emails, one a day

Every member of a workspace gets one short email a day for nine days,
starting the morning after they join, each one step of the Academy, in
order: glance one company, Prospekt it, make the email yours, bring in who
you know, find the person who can walk you in, find a competitor’s clients,
write to one of them, say what happened, and teach it from your calls. Each
is a few lines and one link.

The same nine steps are **Prospektor Academy**, under Learn in
[Settings](/settings/workspace), as four courses: *Your first meeting from a
cold company*, *Get walked in by someone you know*, *Win your competitor’s
customers* and *Make every pitch sharper than the last*. Open a step and it
shows you how, with a button for the screen it is about and **Mark as
done**. A step the studio can see you did is ticked for you, and a step you
mark done there is not emailed to you.

It is not the *product news* box above and does not need it: it goes to you
because you have a workspace, the way a *your run is ready* email does. **One
click on any lesson stops the rest**, without signing in, and a stopped course
does not restart. Sign-in links and emails about your own work are unaffected.

## What your company is called

Your workspace's name goes on every brief, pitch and shared link it produces,
so if it was created from a checkout field, by an agency, or from an uploaded
list, the first owner or admin to sign in is asked to confirm it reads the way
you would write it. Changing it there rewrites your brief, which is what every
pitch is composed from.

If you made the workspace yourself by typing your company name, nobody asks you
again; you already answered.

Once it has been answered, it holds. The studio reads your site again in the
background (when the first research lands, and every time you accept a rescan
months later) and it forms its own opinion about what your company is called
from the way your marketing pages write it. That opinion never overrules yours:
whoever confirmed the name is the last word on it, and a later reading can
change everything else in your brief without touching it. On a workspace nobody
has confirmed yet, the studio's reading is still the better answer and does
replace the name the checkout or the uploaded list came with.

## Your setup call

Getting your brief right is the one thing everything else runs on: the fit
scores, the research, the drafts, the shared links. So on your first arrival at
the front door you are offered **a call to set it up with you**. It is included
in what you already pay, it takes about half an hour, and it is the fastest
route to a pitch you would actually send.

Press **Book a time** on the account card and your own calendar opens on a real
person's availability. If you would rather get on with it, take *Skip for now*:
the offer waits a few days and then asks once more, and it stops asking as soon
as you have saved your first deliverable; at that point you got where the call
was for.

You can ask for one at any time afterwards from the support panel (the same
place you ask a question or request a feature) under **Book a setup call**.
That door does not close when you skip the card, and it does not close once
your workspace is working: a call is worth having whenever you are stuck.

What we record is that the offer was made and what you did with it: a
timestamp, no more. The calendar itself belongs to whoever you booked with; the
studio never sees who else is on it or what is in your diary.

If your studio shows no such offer, this deploy has no calendar attached to it
yet, and there is nothing to book.
